The **Atacama Desert** is a desert plateau in **South America**. Most of it lies in **northern Chile**, though in places it stretches toward southern **Peru**. Many people consider it the **driest non-polar desert in the world**, and some weather stations in its interior have gone years without recording any significant rain. It runs as a narrow north–south strip along the Pacific coast, squeezed between the **Pacific Ocean** to the west and the **Andes Mountains** to the east.

The desert covers roughly **105,000 square kilometres** (about 41,000 sq mi), although broader definitions also take in the arid lands around it. Several things work together to make it so dry. The **cold Humboldt Current** offshore suppresses evaporation and cloud formation. The **subtropical high-pressure system** discourages precipitation. And the Andes keep out moist air from the Amazon Basin. The result is that much of the region gets only a few millimetres of rain a year, and some central areas can go for decades with no measurable precipitation at all.

Even so, life manages to hold on here. The hyper-arid core has very little vegetation, but cacti, shrubs, and hardy grasses grow in the less extreme zones. Coastal fog, known locally as **camanchaca**, supplies moisture that keeps some ecosystems going. Insects, reptiles, birds, and mammals adapted to the dryness live in the desert, and its high-altitude wetlands and salt flats are home to flamingos and other Andean species.

People have lived in the Atacama for a long time. Among the Indigenous peoples are the **Atacameño**, or **Likan Antai**, who built settlements in oases and river valleys. European colonization put the region under Spanish control, and in the 19th century the Atacama became economically important for its rich deposits of **nitrates**, **copper**, and other minerals. Disputes over these resources helped bring about the **War of the Pacific** (1879–1884). Afterward, Chile controlled large areas of desert that had previously belonged to Peru and Bolivia.

Today the Atacama is still a major centre of **mining**, particularly for copper and **lithium**. It also matters a great deal internationally for **astronomy**. High elevation, minimal cloud cover, low humidity, and very little light pollution make it one of the best places on Earth to observe the sky. Major observatories in or near the region include the **Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA)** and several facilities on **Cerro Paranal** and **La Silla**.

The desert is also a significant destination for **tourism** and scientific research. Its dramatic landscapes include salt flats, volcanoes, geysers, and eroded rock formations. Because its dry conditions resemble those on Mars, researchers have used it as an analogue environment for testing space exploration technology and for studying the limits of life in extreme environments.

Moving to a new city feels, at first, like stepping into the life of someone braver than me. The decision usually starts out abstract: a job offer, a school, a relationship, a vague hunger to start over. On paper the move looks clean and purposeful. In practice it's cardboard boxes, forwarded mail, a robotic voice reading out GPS directions, and the small shock of waking up in a room where the light falls differently across the wall. The good and the bad show up together, so tangled up that it's hard to say where one stops and the other starts.

One of the best things about a new city is that it lets you see yourself differently. In the place you've always lived, repetition settles your identity for you. You're someone's kid, someone's friend, the person who gets the usual at the coffee shop or steers clear of certain streets because of old memories. In a new city, nobody knows those stories unless you decide to tell them. That anonymity can be lonely, but it's freeing too. You can be more social or more private. You can try new routines, new neighborhoods, even new versions of your personality. The city doesn't care who you used to be. It only wants to know how you'll get around in it now.

Then there's the plain pleasure of finding things out. Ordinary life turns into a kind of exploration, and buying groceries becomes a minor expedition. You start noticing the architecture, the slang, the weather, how people wait in line or greet strangers. You learn where the best bread is, which park is quietest at dusk, which train platform fills up fastest in the rain. These details pile up slowly, and each one makes the place feel a little less like a map and a little more like home. Moving reminds you that daily life isn't fixed, and that it can still surprise you.

But the costs are real, and they're harder to add up than rent and a moving truck. The obvious one is homesickness, though the word sounds too gentle for what it can be. It isn't only missing people. It's missing the version of yourself that existed so easily around them. In your old city you knew without thinking how to belong. In the new one, belonging is work. You have to build a life almost from scratch: find a doctor, a mechanic, a favorite café, someone to call when something breaks. Even small errands wear you out when you have to do them without the cushion of familiarity.

Then there's the emotional math of distance. Moving usually means accepting that love gets less convenient. Friendships that were held up by living nearby now have to survive on texts, scheduled calls, and pricey visits. Family milestones happen without you, or you go back and find that "home" kept changing while you were gone. The city you left doesn't wait around, preserved for your return. It moves on, just as you do, and there's grief in realizing that.

Still, maybe that's part of what moving is worth. It teaches you that a life only gets bigger by being unsettled. The new city gives you freedom, novelty, and growth, and it bills you in uncertainty, loneliness, and loss. Moving means agreeing to that trade. With time, if you're lucky, the strange streets become your streets. The costs don't go away, but they start to feel less like penalties and more like the price of becoming larger than the life you used to know.

**Major Hospital Network Reports Data Breach Affecting Thousands of Patients**

A large regional hospital network said Tuesday that it's investigating a data breach that may have exposed the personal and medical information of thousands of patients. The disclosure adds to growing worries about cybersecurity weaknesses in healthcare.

The network runs several hospitals, outpatient clinics, and specialty care centers across the region. Earlier this month, it noticed suspicious activity in its computer systems. Officials said in a statement that they moved quickly to contain the problem, started an internal investigation, and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to figure out how far the breach reached.

Early findings suggest that unauthorized actors may have gotten into patient records containing names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, medical record numbers, and insurance details. In some cases, limited clinical information was also included. Officials said they have found no evidence so far that financial account or payment card data was compromised, but the investigation is still going.

"We take the privacy and security of our patients' information extremely seriously," the network said in its statement. "Upon discovering this issue, we immediately implemented containment measures, notified law enforcement, and began working with leading forensic specialists to assess what information may have been affected."

The network didn't say exactly how many patients were involved, though it called the breach "significant." Affected people should expect a letter in the mail within the next few weeks. As a precaution, the organization said it will offer free credit monitoring and identity protection services to eligible patients.

Hospitals have kept operating throughout the investigation, although some administrative systems were temporarily taken offline. That caused delays in scheduling and in access to certain online services. According to officials, emergency departments and inpatient care weren't disrupted.

Cybersecurity experts note that healthcare organizations remain attractive targets for hackers because they hold so much sensitive personal and medical data. A stolen credit card number can be replaced, but medical records can include permanent identifying details that may be used for identity theft, insurance fraud, or phishing attacks.

"This type of incident can have long-lasting consequences for patients," said one data privacy analyst who isn't affiliated with the hospital network. "Even if clinical care is unaffected, the loss of trust can be substantial, especially when health information is involved."

Regulators will likely review the breach under federal health privacy rules, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, or HIPAA. The law requires covered entities to safeguard patient information and to notify individuals when certain breaches occur.

Patients are being advised to watch for unexpected bills, insurance statements, or suspicious emails and phone calls that mention their medical care. The network said it is strengthening system security, reviewing access controls, and taking additional steps to prevent similar incidents in the future.

A good teacher isn't just someone who knows their subject well. Knowledge matters, obviously, but information alone doesn't spark curiosity, build confidence, or change a student's life. To my mind, what makes a good teacher is some mix of patience, passion, empathy, and the knack for making students feel seen. The best ones do more than deliver lessons. They create a space where learning feels possible.

Patience is probably the most important quality. Students don't all learn at the same pace, and no two minds work quite the same way. A good teacher gets that. When a student struggles, they don't get frustrated; they try another explanation, another example, another angle. Patience tells students that difficulty isn't failure and that understanding sometimes takes time. For kids who already doubt themselves, that can make all the difference. A patient teacher teaches more than a subject. They teach perseverance.

Passion is another one. Students can tell when a teacher really cares about what they're teaching, and enthusiasm rubs off. If someone talks about literature, science, history, or math with real interest, even a hard topic can come alive. Passion gives a classroom its energy and turns a list of facts into something meaningful and memorable. Just as important, it shows students that learning doesn't have to be a chore. It can be a source of joy.

Empathy matters just as much. A good teacher remembers what it feels like to be confused, nervous, or scared of getting something wrong. They know students carry burdens nobody can see: trouble at home, stress, insecurity, loneliness, pressure to succeed. So they treat students with kindness and respect. They listen. They notice when someone has gone unusually quiet or seems discouraged. Sometimes the most valuable thing a teacher can give isn't an explanation but a bit of encouragement at the right moment. A student who feels understood is more likely to speak up, take risks, and believe they can improve.

Good teachers also know how to challenge their students, because kindness doesn't mean lowering the bar. Some of the most effective teachers expect a lot precisely because they see what their students are capable of. They push students to think more deeply, work more carefully, and aim higher than they would on their own. It works because the high expectations come with support. They don't just demand excellence; they help students get there.

Finally, a good teacher leaves a mark that reaches beyond the classroom. Years later, students may have forgotten the specific lessons, dates, or formulas, but they usually remember how a teacher made them feel. They remember the one who believed in them when they weren't sure of themselves, who sparked an interest they'd never thought about, or who showed them their voice mattered. In that sense, teaching is about more than education. It's about shaping character and possibility.

So to me, a good teacher is someone who pairs knowledge with humanity. They guide, challenge, encourage, and inspire, and they help students learn not just about the world but about themselves. That's why a truly good teacher can influence someone for a lifetime.

# Commit Message Style Guide

A good commit message helps your teammates review a change, tells whoever maintains the code later why a decision was made, and makes `git log` and `git blame` a lot more useful when you're debugging. Please follow these conventions on every commit.

## Structure

```
<subject line>

<body>

<footer>
```

Put a blank line between the subject and the body. For trivial changes you can skip the body and footer.

## Subject Line

- **Keep it to 50 characters.** 72 is the hard limit.
- **Use the imperative mood.** Write "Add retry logic," not "Added retry logic" or "Adds retry logic." An easy check: the subject should finish the sentence "If applied, this commit will…"
- **Capitalize the first word.**
- **Leave off the trailing period.**
- **Be specific.** "Fix bug" and "Update code" tell the reader nothing, while "Fix null check in user lookup" does.

If your team uses prefixes like `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, or `refactor:` (Conventional Commits), use them consistently, and make sure the whole subject, prefix included, still fits within the limit.

## Body

The body is for explaining **what changed and why**, not how. The diff already shows how. Some questions worth answering:

- What problem led to this change?
- Why did you pick this approach over the alternatives?
- Are there side effects or limitations reviewers should know about?

Wrap lines at 72 characters. If you're listing several separate changes, use bullet points with hyphens or asterisks.

## Footer

The footer is where metadata goes:

- Issue references: `Fixes #123`, `Refs #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: description`
- Co-authors: `Co-authored-by: Name <email>`

## Scope of a Commit

Each commit should be one logical change. If you find yourself needing "and" in the subject, think about splitting it up. Also try not to mix formatting changes with functional ones, because that makes the commit harder to review and harder to revert.

## Examples

**Weak:**
```
fixed stuff
```

**Strong:**
```
Fix race condition in session cleanup

The cleanup job could delete sessions that were being
refreshed concurrently, logging users out unexpectedly.
Acquire a row-level lock before checking expiration.

Fixes #482
```

## Things to Avoid

- Vague messages like "WIP," "misc fixes," or "updates"
- Describing the file rather than the change
- Leaning on context only you have ("as discussed")
- Blaming or editorializing ("fix stupid bug")
- Committing generated noise without explaining it

## Final Check

Before you commit, ask yourself: *Would someone reading this in two years understand why the change was made?* If the answer is no, add more context.

# Tbilisi

**Tbilisi** (Georgian: თბილისი), known historically as **Tiflis**, is Georgia's capital and largest city. It sits on the banks of the Mtkvari (Kura) River, and in the early 2020s about 1.2 million people lived there, roughly a third of the country's population. It is a major cultural, economic, and transportation hub in the South Caucasus.

## History

Tradition holds that King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century AD, after he found warm sulfur springs while out hunting. The name comes from the Old Georgian *tbili*, meaning "warm." Vakhtang's successors moved the royal seat to Tbilisi, and the city kept growing in importance even though Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Mongols, and Turkic dynasties invaded again and again.

Tbilisi flourished during the Georgian Golden Age under King David IV and Queen Tamar, in the 12th and early 13th centuries. It was sacked several times later on, notably by Timur and by the Persian ruler Agha Mohammad Khan in 1795. In the early 19th century the Russian Empire annexed Georgia, and Tbilisi became the administrative center of the Caucasus Viceroyalty. After a brief period of independence from 1918 to 1921, it became the capital of the Georgian Soviet Socialist Republic. Georgia regained its independence in 1991. Since then Tbilisi has been through political upheaval, including the Rose Revolution of 2003, and has also modernized considerably.

## Geography and climate

Tbilisi lies in a valley ringed by mountains and hills, at roughly 400–770 meters above sea level. Its climate is transitional between humid subtropical and continental, with hot summers and cool winters.

## Culture and architecture

The city is known for its eclectic architecture, which mixes medieval, neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet, and contemporary styles. The Old Town (Dzveli Tbilisi) has narrow streets, carved wooden balconies, and the sulfur baths of Abanotubani. Among the best-known landmarks are the Narikala Fortress, the Metekhi Church, the Sioni Cathedral, the Holy Trinity Cathedral (Sameba), and the modern Bridge of Peace. The Kartlis Deda ("Mother of Georgia") statue looks out over the city from Sololaki Ridge.

Tbilisi has plenty of theaters, museums, and festivals, including the Georgian National Museum and the Rustaveli Theatre. Georgian food, such as *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is a big part of the city's identity. Its nightlife and electronic music scene have also drawn international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is the country's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, which opened in 1966, is the main rapid transit system, and buses, minibuses, and a cable car supplement it. Tbilisi International Airport is the country's principal gateway.

## See also

- Georgia (country)
- Kartli
- List of cities in Georgia

Georgian food, such as *khachapuri*, *khinkali*, and local wines, is a big part of the city's identity. Its nightlife and electronic music scene have also drawn international attention.

## Economy and transport

Tbilisi is the country's financial and commercial center. Its main sectors include services, tourism, trade, and manufacturing. The Tbilisi Metro, which opened in 1966, is the main rapid transit system, and buses, minibuses, and a cable car supplement it. Tbilisi International Airport is the country's principal gateway.

# Record Turnout Marks Tuesday's School Board Election in Maplewood County

**Voters surge to the polls in the district's highest-participation off-year race in decades**

MAPLEWOOD — Maplewood County voters showed up in historic numbers Tuesday to choose three school board members. Election officials said 41 percent of registered voters cast ballots, more than double the turnout of the last school board election and the highest for a stand-alone local race in the county's recorded history.

According to the County Elections Office, 38,214 of the district's 93,200 registered voters took part. Two years ago, the figure was roughly 17 percent. Lines stretched out the door at several precincts during the after-work rush, and the polls at Lincoln Elementary stayed open 25 minutes past the scheduled 7 p.m. closing so that everyone already waiting could vote.

"We prepared for a busy day, but nothing like this," said Dolores Whitfield, the county's elections director. "By noon we had already surpassed the total in-person turnout from the last cycle."

Observers pointed to a contentious campaign as the reason. It centered on a proposed budget shortfall, school consolidation plans, and arguments over curriculum and class sizes. Six candidates ran for three open seats. The race drew unusually heavy campaign spending for a local contest, along with a string of packed candidate forums.

Parent groups on both sides of the consolidation debate organized door-knocking efforts and carpools to the polls. In the fall, student volunteers from Maplewood High School also ran a registration drive that added nearly 1,800 new voters to the rolls.

"I've lived here 30 years and never voted in a school board race until this year," said Marcus Delgado, 52, a father of two who waited about 20 minutes to vote at Lincoln Elementary. "Decisions about my kids' classrooms are being made, and I wanted a say."

For others, it was the stakes that got them out. "Closing a school affects the whole neighborhood, not just the families who go there," said Ruth Ann Kessler, a retired teacher.

Preliminary results show incumbent Priya Raman in the lead. Newcomers Thomas Berglund and Angela Ortiz follow, currently holding the other two winning spots. Fewer than 400 votes separate third and fourth place, and the elections office said final results won't be certified until provisional and mail-in ballots are counted next week.

Whitfield said her office will review how the day went so it can be ready for future high-turnout elections. "This is a good problem to have," she said. "We hope it's a sign of lasting engagement."

The new board members will be sworn in at the first meeting of the new year.

**Voyager 1**

**Voyager 1** is a robotic space probe that NASA launched on 5 September 1977 as part of the Voyager program. It was built mainly to study the outer Solar System, and it ended up being one of the most important scientific spacecraft ever made. Once its original mission was finished, it just kept going, and today it is the most distant human-made object from Earth.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built the probe, and it left Cape Canaveral, Florida, on a Titan IIIE rocket. Its twin, **Voyager 2**, actually launched first, but Voyager 1 took a faster route and got to Jupiter and Saturn ahead of it. The mission relied on a rare alignment of the planets, which let spacecraft use gravitational assists to visit several of the outer planets.

Voyager 1's first major encounter was with **Jupiter** in 1979. As it flew by, it sent back detailed images of the planet's atmosphere, from the turbulent cloud bands to the Great Red Spot. It also made key discoveries about Jupiter's moons. Most notably, it found evidence of active volcanism on **Io**, the first time anyone had seen such activity anywhere beyond Earth. It also gathered new information on Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, and on Jupiter's magnetosphere and ring system.

In 1980 the probe passed **Saturn** and its moon **Titan**. Titan was a big priority because of its dense atmosphere. Voyager 1 confirmed that the atmosphere is rich in nitrogen, but the opaque haze kept it from getting detailed images of the surface. It also sent back extensive observations of Saturn's rings, moons, and magnetic environment. The trajectory needed for the Titan flyby threw the spacecraft out of the plane of the Solar System, which ended any chance of further planetary encounters.

Once the planetary mission was over, Voyager 1 moved into an extended mission to study the outer heliosphere, the region shaped by the solar wind. In August 2012, NASA announced that it had become the first spacecraft to enter **interstellar space**, crossing the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's influence gives way to the interstellar medium. Since then, its instruments have kept measuring charged particles, magnetic fields, and plasma conditions in a region scientists still understand poorly.

Voyager 1 also carries a **Golden Record**, a phonograph record of sounds, images, and messages meant to show the diversity of life and culture on Earth. It was conceived as a symbolic message to anyone who might find it in the future, and it has become one of the mission's most lasting cultural legacies.

In the 21st century, Voyager 1 is still in contact with Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network, though its power supply slowly declines as its radioisotope thermoelectric generators lose output. The mission has been extended again and again, and the probe continues to return valuable scientific data as it travels deeper into interstellar space.

## Pivot Tables User Guide

A pivot table lets you summarize and analyze large sets of spreadsheet data quickly. You don't have to sort, filter, or write formulas by hand. Just use a pivot table to group information, calculate totals, and spot trends.

### When to Use a Pivot Table
Reach for a pivot table when you want to:
- Total sales by region, product, or salesperson
- Count records, like customers or orders
- Compare values across categories
- Rearrange data without touching the original table
- Look for patterns in large datasets

### Before You Begin
You'll get the best results if your source data:
- Is laid out in rows and columns
- Has just one header row
- Has no completely blank rows or columns
- Keeps data types consistent within each column, whether dates, numbers, or text

Typical source columns might be `Date`, `Region`, `Product`, `Salesperson`, `Units`, and `Revenue`.

### Creating a Pivot Table
1. Click any cell in your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and pick **Pivot Table**.
3. Confirm the data range.
4. Decide where the pivot table should go:
   - A new worksheet
   - An existing worksheet
5. Click **Create** or **OK**.

You'll see a blank pivot table layout along with a field list.

### Understanding the Pivot Table Areas
Most pivot-table tools have four layout areas:

- **Rows**: Shows categories running vertically
- **Columns**: Shows categories running horizontally
- **Values**: Shows calculations such as sum, count, or average
- **Filters**: Lets you limit the data that's shown

### Building a Basic Pivot Table
To see total revenue by region:
1. Drag **Region** to **Rows**.
2. Drag **Revenue** to **Values**.

The pivot table then lists each region with its total revenue.

To compare revenue by region and product:
1. Leave **Region** in **Rows**.
2. Drag **Product** to **Columns**.
3. Leave **Revenue** in **Values**.

### Changing Calculations
You can usually summarize a value field in several ways, including:
- Sum
- Count
- Average
- Minimum
- Maximum

To change the calculation:
1. Click the value field in the pivot table or in the field settings.
2. Open **Value Field Settings** or **Summarize By**.
3. Pick the calculation you need.

### Filtering and Sorting
To refine your results, you can:
- Apply a report filter, for example to show only one year
- Sort row labels alphabetically or by value
- Expand or collapse grouped items

### Refreshing the Pivot Table
When the source data changes, refresh the pivot table so the results update:
1. Click anywhere in the pivot table.
2. Choose **Refresh** from the pivot-table toolbar or the context menu.

### Tips
- Give your source columns clear names
- Format numbers so they're easy to read, such as currency or percentages
- If dates won't group properly, make sure they're stored as real dates
- Leave the source data as it is and do your analysis in the pivot table

Pivot tables are powerful because they let you reorganize data instantly, which makes reporting and decision-making faster and easier.

# Pivot Tables: A User Guide

## What Is a Pivot Table?

A pivot table lets you summarize a big dataset without writing any formulas. You can group, count, total, and average your data, then rearrange it in seconds to look at it from a different angle. It's the tool to reach for when you're asking things like "What were total sales by region?" or "How many orders did each rep close per month?"

## Before You Begin

Get your data in shape first:

- **Include headers.** Every column needs its own unique title, and none can be blank.
- **Avoid blank rows or columns.** They can make the table miss some of your data.
- **Keep data consistent.** Each column should hold just one kind of information, like only dates or only numbers.

## Creating a Pivot Table

1. Click any cell inside your data range.
2. Open the **Insert** menu and choose **Pivot Table**.
3. Check that the data range shown is the right one.
4. Pick a destination. A new sheet is recommended, but you can use an existing location instead.
5. Click **OK** or **Create**.

You'll see an empty pivot table, plus a field panel that lists your column headers.

## Understanding the Four Areas

The field panel has four boxes. Drag fields into them to build your report.

- **Rows:** Categories that run down the left side (Product, for example).
- **Columns:** Categories that run across the top (such as Quarter).
- **Values:** The numbers being calculated (for example, Sum of Revenue).
- **Filters:** Fields that let you narrow the whole table to certain items, like a single year.

## Example

Say your data has columns for Region, Salesperson, Month, and Revenue, and you want to see revenue by region and month:

1. Drag **Region** to Rows.
2. Drag **Month** to Columns.
3. Drag **Revenue** to Values.

Now the table shows total revenue for every region-month combination, with grand totals along the edges.

## Changing the Calculation

Numeric fields are summed by default. If you want something else, click the field in the Values box, select **Value Field Settings**, and pick another function, such as Count, Average, Max, or Min. You can also show values as a percentage of the total.

## Refining Your Report

- **Sort:** Click the dropdown arrow next to a row or column label.
- **Filter:** Use that same arrow to uncheck any items you want to hide.
- **Group:** Right-click dates to group them by month, quarter, or year.
- **Rearrange:** Drag fields from one area to another to see the data differently.

## Keeping Data Current

A pivot table won't update on its own when the source data changes. Right-click the table and select **Refresh**. If you've added new rows, you might also need to update the source range under **Change Data Source**.

## Troubleshooting

- **Numbers counted instead of summed:** The column probably has text or blanks in it. Clean up the data and refresh.
- **Dates won't group:** Some entries may be stored as text. Convert them to true dates.

Give it a little practice, and pivot tables will become one of the quickest ways you have to analyze data.

# What the Walls Remember

When I was nine, my grandmother took me to the train station in the town where she grew up. It had been closed for decades. The windows were clouded over and the ticket counter had long ago lost its brass. She walked into the waiting room and laid her palm flat against the wall, the way you'd check a sleeping animal to see if it was still breathing. "I left for the city from this bench," she told me. "Your grandfather proposed on that platform." By any architect's standards it was an ordinary building. For her, her whole life had turned on it.

I think of that whenever someone says old buildings are just obstacles: expensive to maintain, a pain to retrofit, taking up room where something shinier could go. It's not a stupid argument. Old buildings leak. They fight you on the wiring. Plenty of them don't meet current codes, and sentiment won't pay for a new roof. I don't think every old structure needs saving, either. Surviving doesn't make a building sacred.

Still, some of them are worth it, and I've come to think the reasons are practical as well as sentimental.

For one, an old building holds a kind of memory an archive can't. A photograph tells you what a street looked like, but a building lets you stand inside proportions that people once thought were normal. You notice how low the ceilings were and how narrow the stairs, and how much the light came from windows instead of switches. History stops being abstract when you have to duck to get through its doorway.

They also carry craftsmanship we mostly don't pay for anymore. The library in my hometown is a century old, and I practically lived there as a teenager. Someone had carved little acorns into the banister. Nobody made them do it, and no budget meeting would sign off on it today. But generations of restless kids ran their hands over those acorns, and I suspect it taught us, without anyone saying a word, that ordinary places could be built with care.

Then there's continuity. A neighborhood made entirely of new construction can feel strangely weightless, like a stage set waiting for the play to start. Old buildings make a place feel lived in. A newcomer and a lifelong resident can share a landmark even if they remember it differently. That common reference point is one of the threads holding a community together, and it's a lot easier to tear fabric than to weave it.

And there's the simple matter of waste. Preservationists like to say the greenest building is the one that's already standing, and they have a point. Tearing a building down throws away the energy and materials already in it, and fills landfills on top of that.

The train station was eventually torn down for a parking lot. Last year I drove through town and tried to find where the bench had been. I couldn't. The asphalt was smooth, the painted lines were crisp, and nothing suggested anyone had ever proposed or left from that spot.

That's what I'd like the skeptics to understand. We don't save buildings because stone and timber are precious. We save them because they hold the places where our lives took shape, and when they go, the bench goes too, and the palm against the wall, and the proof.

The Battle of Hastings was fought on 14 October 1066 between William, Duke of Normandy, and King Harold Godwinson of England. It was the decisive battle of the Norman Conquest of England and led to Norman rule there. The battle is traditionally named after the nearby town of Hastings, but it actually took place about 7 miles (11 km) to the northwest, close to the present town of Battle in East Sussex.

The fight grew out of a disputed succession. When Edward the Confessor died in January 1066, Harold Godwinson was crowned king. William, however, claimed that Edward had promised him the throne earlier and that Harold had sworn to support that claim. A third claimant, Harald Hardrada of Norway, also invaded England. Harold Godwinson defeated and killed him at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, but the victory left his army exhausted.

In the meantime, William crossed the English Channel and landed at Pevensey on 28 September 1066. He marched into Sussex, built a prefabricated castle at Hastings, and raided the surrounding countryside, partly to draw Harold south. Harold hurried down from London with his household troops, the housecarls, and the levies of the shires, known as the fyrd.

The armies met on Senlac Hill. Harold's men formed a dense shield wall along the ridge, while William's army, in keeping with Norman military practice, was made up of infantry, archers, and cavalry. The battle lasted most of the day and was hard fought. The English line repelled the first Norman assaults. At one point, rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have lifted his helmet to show he was alive and to rally his troops.

The crucial turning point came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while pursuing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were genuine or feigned, but either way they let the Norman cavalry isolate and destroy sections of Harold's army. Late in the day Harold himself was killed. Tradition says an arrow struck him in the eye, though how he actually died is uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility slain, resistance collapsed.

William's victory paved the way for his coronation as King William I of England on 25 December 1066. The battle transformed English society, aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. It is memorialized in sources such as the Bayeux Tapestry, one of the most important visual records of the conquest.

Harold hurried down from London with his household troops, the housecarls, and the levies of the shires, known as the fyrd.

The armies met on Senlac Hill. Harold's men formed a dense shield wall along the ridge, while William's army, in keeping with Norman military practice, was made up of infantry, archers, and cavalry. The battle lasted most of the day and was hard fought. The English line repelled the first Norman assaults. At one point, rumors spread that William had been killed, but he is said to have lifted his helmet to show he was alive and to rally his troops.

The crucial turning point came when parts of the English line broke formation, possibly while pursuing retreating Normans. Historians still debate whether those retreats were genuine or feigned, but either way they let the Norman cavalry isolate and destroy sections of Harold's army. Late in the day Harold himself was killed. Tradition says an arrow struck him in the eye, though how he actually died is uncertain. With the king dead and much of the English nobility slain, resistance collapsed.

William's victory paved the way for his coronation as King William I of England on 25 December 1066. The battle transformed English society, aristocracy, language, and government, and tied England more closely to continental Europe. It is memorialized in sources such as the Bayeux Tapestry, one of the most important visual records of the conquest.

# Transit Strike Halts Buses and Trains, Leaving Thousands of Commuters Stranded

**Union rejects final offer as talks collapse overnight; city braces for second day of disruption**

Hundreds of thousands of commuters had to find another way around Monday after public-transit workers walked off the job at dawn and shut down bus and rail service across the metropolitan region.

The Metro Transit Workers Union represents about 8,200 drivers, mechanics, and station staff. Its members went on strike at 4 a.m., hours after contract talks with the Regional Transit Authority fell apart late Sunday. No one has seen a systemwide work stoppage here in 14 years.

"We didn't want to be here," said union president Dolores Reyes, standing at a picket line outside the Eastside bus depot. "But you can't ask the people who keep this city moving to fall behind on rent while costs go up every year."

The union wants a 9 percent raise over three years, better protection against assaults on drivers, and limits on mandatory overtime. The Authority offered a 5 percent raise instead. Officials said they couldn't meet the other demands without raising fares or cutting routes.

"Our offer was fair and fiscally responsible," Authority spokesperson Martin Vail said in a statement. "We remain at the table and urge the union to return to negotiations so riders can get back to their lives."

The effects showed up right away. Highways were clogged before sunrise, and traffic officials reported delays as much as 70 percent longer than normal. Ride-share prices jumped, and by 8 a.m. the bike-share stations in the downtown core had been emptied. Several large employers told staff to work from home.

Central Station is usually packed in the morning. This time a handful of people stood around reading the posted closure notices. Marcus Hill, who works in a hospital cafeteria, said he walked two miles before he found a friend who could drive him the rest of the way.

"I support the drivers, I really do," Hill said. "But I can't afford to miss shifts either. I'm stuck in the middle."

Schools saw more absences than usual. The district said yellow school buses are still running because a separate contractor operates them. Paratransit service for riders with disabilities is running at limited capacity under an emergency agreement, although advocates say waits have stretched past two hours.

Mayor Elaine Cho urged both sides to get back to the table right away and offered city staff to serve as mediators. "Every day this continues costs working families and local businesses," she said.

Economists estimate the shutdown could cost the regional economy $30 million a day in lost productivity and sales.

No new negotiating session has been scheduled. The union says it will keep picketing until it gets a "serious proposal." The Authority says it is making contingency plans for a prolonged stoppage.

I don't think old buildings deserve to be saved just for being old. Age isn't a virtue. A cracked wall or a faded sign doesn't become meaningful because it happened to survive. But some buildings hold more than their own bricks. They hold memory, fine craftsmanship, a sense of who a place is, and a record of how people once pictured their lives. To me, preserving them isn't about freezing the past. It's about keeping a conversation going between generations.

I tend to think of old buildings as public memory. Families hang on to photo albums, letters, and heirlooms because objects can carry feeling in a way facts can't, and towns and cities need that too. A preserved train station, schoolhouse, church, or row of apartments can tell us more about the people who built a place than any plaque will. Think of the width of a staircase, the hand-carved trim around a doorway, the dip worn into stone steps. They remind us that history was lived in bodies. Somebody climbed those stairs every day. Somebody stood in that hallway waiting for news, for work, for love, or for grief to pass. When those buildings go, a piece of our shared memory goes with them.

They're also beautiful in a way that's hard to reproduce. A lot of them were built patiently, with durable materials and a degree of ornament that came from pride rather than efficiency. Even plain ones show a human hand: uneven bricks laid one at a time, wood floors polished by decades of footsteps, windows placed for grace as much as function. So much construction now is driven by speed and profit, and these buildings show that usefulness and beauty don't have to fight each other. They teach us to care about texture, permanence, and detail.

There's an ethical side, too. Tearing down and rebuilding isn't always progress. Sometimes it's amnesia dressed up as development. That said, not every old building can or should be saved. Cities have to change, and communities need housing, safety, and accessibility. But when a building has real architectural distinction or deep cultural importance, saving it is a way of showing respect. It says the people who came before us aren't disposable, and that the struggles and achievements that shaped a neighborhood still count. That matters most for places tied to ordinary people rather than the rich or famous. A factory, a corner store, or a union hall may tell a more democratic story than any mansion.

What moves me most is how preserved buildings make time feel layered instead of lost. Walk into an old library or courthouse and, even for a moment, you feel your own life is part of a longer human story. The building has outlasted fashions, governments, and private worries. It has seen generations come and go and is still standing, asking for care rather than pity. At its best, preservation is an act of humility. It admits we're not the first people to love a place, and we won't be the last who need something solid to remember it by.

# Contributing to the Docs

Thanks for helping improve our documentation! Whether you're fixing a typo or writing a whole new tutorial, your work makes the project easier to use. Here's how to get started.

## Ways to contribute

- **Fix errors.** Typos, broken links, outdated screenshots, and incorrect code samples are all fair game.
- **Improve clarity.** Rewrite explanations that confuse you, or add context that's missing.
- **Write new content.** We need tutorials, how-to guides, and reference pages.
- **Review pull requests.** Fresh eyes catch things the rest of us miss.
- **Report issues.** If you spot a problem but can't fix it yourself, open an issue.

## Getting set up

1. Fork the repository and clone your fork locally.
2. Run `npm install` to install dependencies.
3. Run `npm run dev` to start the local preview server.
4. Open `http://localhost:3000` and your changes will update live as you edit.

If all you need is a small edit, you can skip the setup. Click **Edit this page** at the bottom of any page and make the change directly on GitHub.

## Making a change

1. Create a branch with a descriptive name, like `fix-install-typo` or `add-auth-guide`.
2. Make your edits in the `docs/` directory. The files are Markdown.
3. Run `npm run lint` to check formatting, then `npm run build` to make sure the site builds without broken links.
4. Commit with a clear message, for example `Fix incorrect flag in CLI reference`.
5. Push your branch and open a pull request.

## Style guidelines

Consistent writing makes the docs easier to read, so please follow these conventions:

- **Use plain language.** Keep sentences short and skip unnecessary jargon.
- **Address the reader as "you."**
- **Use active voice.** Write "Run the command," not "The command should be run."
- **Put code in code blocks,** and specify the language so it gets syntax highlighting.
- **Use sentence case for headings.**
- **Make examples runnable.** Test every snippet before you submit it.
- **Write descriptive link text.** Avoid "click here."

## Structure of the docs

We sort content into four types:

- **Tutorials:** step-by-step lessons for beginners.
- **How-to guides:** solutions to specific problems.
- **Reference:** precise technical descriptions.
- **Explanations:** background and concepts.

Try to keep each page focused on just one of these.

## Pull request checklist

Before you submit, make sure that:

- [ ] The site builds locally without errors.
- [ ] Links and code samples work.
- [ ] Your changes follow the style guidelines.
- [ ] The PR description explains what changed and why.

## Review process

A maintainer will usually respond within a few days. We may suggest edits, but please don't take that as discouragement. Feedback is a normal part of working together. Once your PR is approved, your changes get merged and published automatically.

## Community expectations

Be kind, patient, and respectful. All contributors must follow our Code of Conduct.

## Need help?

Ask questions in our discussion forum or comment on an issue. We're happy to help first-time contributors get started.

The **Hanseatic League** was a commercial and defensive alliance of merchant guilds and market towns across northwestern and central Europe. From the late 12th century to the 17th, it dominated maritime trade in the Baltic and North Seas. At its peak it tied together nearly 200 towns, reaching from London and Bruges in the west to Novgorod and Bergen in the east and north, and it shaped the economic, political, and urban development of medieval northern Europe in a big way.

It began with German merchants, especially those from cities like Lübeck and Hamburg, who wanted protection and privileges when they traded abroad. Lübeck was founded in 1143 and sat in a strategic spot between the North and Baltic Seas, which made it the League's leading city. By the 13th century, merchant communities from German-speaking towns had set up trading outposts called *Kontore* in major foreign centers, including London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod. These settlements worked as warehouses, offices, and legal communities that looked after Hanseatic interests.

The League was not a state. It had no formal constitution, no permanent army, and no centralized administration. It was a loose association of towns and merchants held together by shared economic interests. Decisions were made at assemblies called the *Hansetag*, where delegates from member cities hammered out commercial policy, mutual defense, and relations with foreign rulers. Membership was fluid, and how much a city took part varied.

Its economic strength came from trading regional goods. Grain, timber, wax, fur, and fish came from the east, while cloth, wine, salt, and metal goods came from the west and south. Hanseatic merchants built efficient shipping networks and standardized their commercial practices, which cut transaction costs and built trust over long distances. When needed, the League also used embargoes and naval force to defend its privileges, as in its conflicts with Denmark in the 14th century.

From the late 15th century on, the League slowly declined. Stronger territorial states were emerging, trade routes were shifting toward the Atlantic, Dutch and English competition was growing, and internal divisions sapped its influence. Its overseas trading privileges were gradually whittled down, and several *Kontore* closed. Some cities still identified with the League, but by the 17th century its political significance had largely vanished. The last *Hansetag* met in 1669.

The League left a lasting mark on the urban culture, architecture, and commercial law of northern Europe. Many former Hanseatic cities, among them Lübeck, Hamburg, Bremen, and Tallinn, still have distinctive brick Gothic buildings and civic traditions tied to the League. Historians today often see it as an early example of transnational commercial cooperation and urban networking in European history.

# Bike-Share FAQ

## Getting Started

**How do I rent a bike?**
Download our app and create an account. Then find a station near you, tap "Unlock," and scan the QR code on the bike. If you'd rather not use the app, you can also unlock a bike at a station kiosk with a credit card.

**How much does it cost?**
- **Single ride:** $1 to unlock, plus $0.15 per minute
- **Day pass:** $12 for unlimited 30-minute rides over 24 hours
- **Monthly membership:** $20 for unlimited 45-minute rides
- **Annual membership:** $150 for unlimited 45-minute rides

We offer discounted memberships for students, seniors, and low-income residents. You can apply on our website.

## Using the Service

**How long can I keep a bike?**
As long as you like, but any time beyond the minutes included in your plan is billed at $0.15 per minute. If you're going on a longer trip, dock the bike and check out another one to reset your time.

**Where can I return my bike?**
Any station with an open dock will do. Push the front wheel firmly into the dock until the light turns green. If the station is full, use the app to find the nearest one with space, and you'll get a free 10-minute extension.

**Do I need to bring a helmet?**
We don't provide helmets, but we strongly recommend wearing one. If you're under 16, the law requires it.

**Are electric bikes available?**
Yes. E-bikes have a green stripe and cost an extra $0.10 per minute. They assist you up to 20 mph.

## Safety and Problems

**What if a bike is damaged?**
Before you ride, check the brakes, tires, and seat. If something seems off, press the red "Report" button on the bike's screen or report it through the app. Then return the bike to a dock so it can be taken out of service. Rides under one minute aren't charged.

**What if the bike is lost or stolen?**
Whenever you stop, lock the bike with its built-in cable lock. For short stops, you can use the "Hold" feature in the app. If a bike is lost or stolen while it's in your care, report it within 24 hours. Losses that aren't reported may result in a $250 fee.

**Can I ride at night?**
Yes. The bikes have built-in front and rear lights that turn on automatically.

## Account Help

**Can I share my membership?**
No. Memberships are personal, and each account can unlock only one bike at a time. If you're riding in a group, everyone will need their own account.

**How do I cancel my membership?**
In the app, go to Settings > Membership and select "Cancel." Monthly plans end when the billing period closes, and annual plans can be refunded within 14 days.

**Who do I contact for help?**
You can call 555-0142, email help@citybikeshare.example, or use the in-app chat. Support is available every day from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

## Plugin System

The editor has a plugin system that lets you extend its core functionality without touching the main application. With plugins, you can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin Structure

Every plugin gets its own directory, and that directory has to contain a manifest file called `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

`plugin.json` holds the plugin's metadata and points to its entry script:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: A unique identifier for the plugin.
- `name`: A human-readable name.
- `version`: The plugin's version.
- `main`: The entry script the editor loads.

You can also include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies` if you want.

### Lifecycle

On startup, the editor scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads the plugins that are enabled. The entry script has to export an `activate` function. It can also export a `deactivate` function, which is called when the plugin is unloaded or when the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

`activate` is the place to register commands, subscribe to events, or set up UI elements. `deactivate` is where you dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins talk to the editor through the `api` object that gets passed into `activate`. The common namespaces are:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

Here's an example of registering a command:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and Management

To install a plugin, copy its directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder, or use the built-in plugin manager. From the settings interface, users can enable, disable, update, or remove plugins.

When a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and keeps starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues all show up in the developer console.

### Best Practices

- Give each plugin one focused responsibility.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs like `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings, and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners when the plugin deactivates.
- Don't run blocking operations during activation, so startup stays fast.

## Plugin System

The editor has a plugin system that lets you extend its core functionality without touching the main application. With plugins, you can add commands, sidebar panels, language support, formatters, themes, and event-driven behavior.

### Plugin Structure

Every plugin gets its own directory, and that directory has to contain a manifest file called `plugin.json`. A typical plugin looks like this:

```text
my-plugin/
  plugin.json
  main.js
  README.md
  assets/
```

`plugin.json` holds the plugin's metadata and points to its entry script:

```json
{
  "id": "example.hello-world",
  "name": "Hello World",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "main.js",
  "enabled": true
}
```

Required fields:

- `id`: A unique identifier for the plugin.
- `name`: A human-readable name.
- `version`: The plugin's version.
- `main`: The entry script the editor loads.

You can also include `description`, `author`, and `dependencies` if you want.

### Lifecycle

On startup, the editor scans the plugin directory, reads each manifest, and loads the plugins that are enabled. The entry script has to export an `activate` function. It can also export a `deactivate` function, which is called when the plugin is unloaded or when the editor exits.

Example:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("hello.sayHello", () => {
    api.window.showMessage("Hello from plugin!");
  });
}

export function deactivate() {
  // Clean up resources here
}
```

`activate` is the place to register commands, subscribe to events, or set up UI elements. `deactivate` is where you dispose of timers, listeners, and temporary state.

### Editor API

Plugins talk to the editor through the `api` object that gets passed into `activate`. The common namespaces are:

- `api.commands`: Register and execute commands.
- `api.window`: Show notifications, dialogs, and UI panels.
- `api.workspace`: Access open files, project folders, and settings.
- `api.editor`: Read or modify the active document.
- `api.events`: Subscribe to editor events such as file open, save, or cursor movement.

Here's an example of registering a command:

```js
export function activate(api) {
  api.commands.register("example.insertDate", () => {
    const editor = api.editor.getActiveEditor();
    if (!editor) return;

    editor.insertText(new Date().toLocaleDateString());
  });
}
```

### Installation and Management

To install a plugin, copy its directory into the editor's `plugins/` folder, or use the built-in plugin manager. From the settings interface, users can enable, disable, update, or remove plugins.

When a plugin fails to load, the editor logs the error and keeps starting up. Load errors, activation failures, and dependency issues all show up in the developer console.

### Best Practices

- Give each plugin one focused responsibility.
- Use stable, namespaced command IDs like `author.feature.action`.
- Validate settings, and handle missing editor state gracefully.
- Dispose of event listeners when the plugin deactivates.
- Don't run blocking operations during activation, so startup stays fast.

A well-designed plugin feels native to the editor, stays lightweight, and fails safely when the context it needs isn't available.

# The Gift of Having Nothing to Do

Last summer my phone died on a train, and I was stuck with four hours of countryside and nothing to look at but the window. For the first twenty minutes I was close to frantic. My hand kept going to my pocket, the way your tongue keeps going to a missing tooth. I counted fence posts. I reread the safety instructions above the door. I was bored, plain and simple.

Then, somewhere past a river I never learned the name of, something changed. My mind quit scrambling for input and started making its own. I remembered a conversation with my grandmother that I hadn't thought about in years. I worked out how to restructure a project at work that had been nagging at me for weeks. For no reason at all, I made up a whole backstory for the man asleep across the aisle. By the time we pulled into the station I felt oddly rested, like I'd actually been somewhere.

I think about that trip a lot, because it made me see what I've been giving up. Boredom used to be unavoidable. It lived in waiting rooms, on long car rides, in that dead hour between homework and dinner. Now I can get rid of it completely. Any gap in the day can be filled with a feed, a podcast, a scroll. I've gotten so good at escaping boredom that I've nearly forgotten what it was for.

I've come to believe it's a kind of internal housekeeping. When nothing is demanding our attention, the mind turns inward and starts sorting. It links things that don't obviously go together. It brings up the worries we've been outrunning and the desires we haven't admitted to. Psychologists have tied this idle wandering to creativity and planning, which fits what I've seen. My best ideas have never shown up while I was consuming something. They come in the shower, on walks, while I'm washing dishes, in the unguarded edges of the day.

Boredom also teaches you what you want, which sounds odd but seems true to me. If I'm bored long enough, I find out what I actually want to do instead of what I'm just being offered. As a kid, summer boredom eventually pushed me to build a fort, start a terrible comic, or take apart a broken radio. Nobody handed me those projects. They grew out of the discomfort of an empty afternoon, and they felt like mine in a way entertainment never does.

I don't want to romanticize it. Boredom is unpleasant, and that's the point. It's a signal, like hunger, that part of us wants something to engage with. The mistake is answering it with whatever's closest. Fast food quiets hunger without nourishing you, and a scroll quiets boredom without giving your mind anything to chew on.

So I've started a small practice. I leave my phone in my bag when I'm waiting in line. I take walks without headphones. Sometimes I sit on the porch and just watch the light change on the neighbor's maple. The first few minutes are always itchy. Then, almost every time, the restlessness gives way to something roomier, and thoughts I didn't know I was carrying start to surface.

I used to think an empty moment was a wasted one. Now I think it's more like fallow ground. It looks like nothing is happening, but it's where the next thing is getting ready to grow.

**The Weight of a Hamburger**

When I was nine, I watched my uncle kill a pig. I'd been told to stay in the truck, and of course I didn't. The blood isn't what stuck with me. It's how quiet things got afterward, and how ordinary the men seemed once it was over, rinsing their hands and talking about the weather. We had pork shoulder that night. It was delicious, and I couldn't stop thinking about the pig's eyes.

I've been circling that evening ever since.

For years I dodged the question the way you dodge a bill you're pretty sure you can't pay. I ate chicken breasts that came in plastic, shaped like nothing that had ever been alive. Then I read a book about industrial farming, the kind written to wreck your appetite, and it did. I went vegetarian for three years. I meant it, and I was a little insufferable about it.

I believed then, and still do, that suffering matters. Pigs are smart and social, and they feel fear. If I grant that a dog's pain counts, I have to explain why a pig's wouldn't, and "because it tastes good" is a lousy answer. Most of the world's meat comes from animals kept in conditions I'd call cruel if I saw them inflicted on anything I loved. I can't argue my way around that anymore, so I've quit trying.

What wore down was the certainty I had as a vegetarian. The arguments didn't get weaker. Life just got messier. I spent a winter with relatives who ate mostly what they raised and hunted, and their relationship to meat looked nothing like mine. They knew the animals, thanked them without any embarrassment, and wasted nothing. I honestly couldn't say they were doing worse than I was, standing in a grocery aisle buying almond milk shipped from a drought-stricken valley. Every way of eating costs something. What matters is whether you can see the cost.

That's where I've ended up, and I'm not comfortable there. To me the worst part of modern meat isn't that animals die. It's that the dying has been hidden from us, and distance makes cruelty easy. If I'm going to eat an animal, I ought to be willing to know where it lived and how it was killed. And if I can't stand to know, that tells me something too.

These days I eat meat rarely and try to know where it comes from. I buy from a farmer whose fields I've walked through. Sometimes I slip, grabbing whatever's convenient at an airport or a wedding, and I feel the old pang. I don't think that makes me virtuous. Maybe it just makes me a more thoughtful participant in something I can't fully justify.

I used to want a clean answer, a rule to follow or a principle that would let me stop thinking about it. I don't trust that wish anymore. Some questions are supposed to stay a little open and keep nagging at you.

I still think about the pig now and then. I don't believe the memory is telling me to stop eating, exactly. It's telling me to stay awake while I do.

**Svalbard Global Seed Vault**

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** sits on **Spitsbergen**, a Norwegian island in the **Svalbard archipelago**, roughly 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole. It opened in **2008** to hold duplicate samples of seeds from gene banks around the world. The idea is to protect crop diversity against loss from war, natural disasters, equipment failure, climate change, or poor management.

The vault is tunneled into the side of **Platåberget**, a sandstone mountain near the settlement of **Longyearbyen**. The remote Arctic site was picked for political and environmental reasons. Svalbard is geologically stable, and its cold climate and the surrounding permafrost help keep the seeds safe even if the power goes out. Seeds are stored at about **−18 °C (0 °F)**, a standard temperature for long-term conservation in seed banks.

People often call it the world's "**doomsday vault**," but it works as a backup repository, not a conventional seed bank. It doesn't own the seeds kept there. They stay the property of the institutions that deposited them, under a "black box" arrangement in which only the depositors have the right to access their own collections. The point is to support national, regional, and international gene banks by giving them an extra layer of security.

Norway's government developed the vault in partnership with the **Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen)** and the **Crop Trust**. It can hold millions of seed samples covering a huge range of food crops and their wild relatives, including varieties of wheat, rice, maize, barley, beans, and many other agriculturally important species. Preserving this genetic diversity is considered essential for future plant breeding, food security, and adapting to changing environmental conditions.

The vault has proved useful in practice, too. In **2015**, the **International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA)** became the first institution to withdraw seeds from it, after conflict in Syria disrupted work at its regional gene bank. The seeds were used to regenerate the collections, and fresh samples were later redeposited. It showed the vault doing what it was meant to do, serving as a global insurance policy for agriculture.

Since opening, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault has become an international symbol of efforts to preserve biodiversity and secure the genetic foundations of the world's food supply. Many regard it as one of the most important facilities for the long-term conservation of crop diversity.

**The Weight of Paper**

When my grandmother died, I found her letters in a shoebox, rubber-banded by year. Some of mine were in there too, dutiful little notes from childhood about school and a lost tooth, and she'd held onto them for decades. But I kept going back to her side of it, the letters my mother had saved and later handed to me.

Nothing much happens in them. The tomatoes are coming in late. Mrs. Dolan's hip is no better. It rained Tuesday, and then Wednesday, and then, she wrote, "it seemed to lose interest." I laughed out loud at that, alone in my kitchen, hearing her dry voice in the slanted blue ink. Somewhere she had crossed out a word and put another above it, and I could picture her stopping, thinking, and making up her mind. That tiny correction told me more about her than any photograph has.

I think that's what we give up when we stop writing letters. It isn't the information. It's the proof of attention. A letter means someone sat down and kept you in their head for twenty uninterrupted minutes, not while waiting on coffee or half-watching TV. They picked a page and a pen and you. These days I send dozens of messages a day. They're quick and warm and useful, and they weigh nothing. They show up while I'm distracted and get answered while the other person is distracted too. Hardly any of them are kept. How would you even keep them?

Letters also demanded a patience that changed what people said. You couldn't fire off a feeling and take it back ten seconds later. You had to let a thought run its course, and sometimes it turned into something else along the way. In that shoebox I found a three-page letter my grandfather wrote my grandmother about a quarrel, and its last paragraph contradicts the first. He hadn't set out to forgive her. The writing took him there. A text would have left him angry, or ended the whole thing with one curt word.

Then there was the waiting. Now we treat waiting as a pure cost, a flaw to be engineered out. But those days between sending and receiving gave longing a place to live. You walked to the mailbox carrying a small private hope. And when something did come, it had traveled to get to you. It had a stamp, a smudge, a faint smell of someone else's house.

Last winter I wrote to an old friend who had moved across the country. It took an hour and a half, much longer than I'd figured, because I kept running into things I hadn't known I wanted to say. My handwriting had gone ragged from lack of use. I crossed out a word and wrote another above it. When I dropped the envelope into the box I felt strangely exposed, as if I'd given away something I couldn't edit.

She wrote back three weeks later. I still have her letter on my desk, the paper slightly creased where her hand pressed down. Among other things, it says that it has been raining, and that the rain seems to have lost interest.

# Design Proposal: Caching Layer for Web API

## Overview
I'm proposing we add a caching layer to the web API. The aim is to cut response latency, ease the load on our backend, and help us scale. The cache would hold frequently requested API responses and serve them directly, so we don't have to hit the database or downstream services every time.

## Goals
- Bring down average API response time
- Reduce load on the database and services
- Handle traffic spikes with better throughput
- Keep data reasonably fresh
- Give us visibility into how the cache behaves

## Non-Goals
- Replacing the primary database
- Caching highly sensitive or user-specific data without additional controls
- Guaranteeing perfectly fresh data on every endpoint

## Architecture
The cache would sit between the API application and the backend data sources. When a request comes in, the API checks the cache first. If there's a valid entry, it gets returned right away. If not, the API pulls the data from the source, returns the response, and writes it to the cache.

I recommend a distributed in-memory store like Redis, since it has low latency, supports expiration, and is operationally mature. For static or public GET endpoints, we could also add a CDN or edge cache later.

## Cache Strategy
We'll start with **cache-aside**, which works like this:
1. The client requests a resource
2. The API looks up the cache key
3. On a hit, it returns the cached response
4. On a miss, it fetches from the backend
5. It stores the result in the cache with a TTL
6. It returns the response

It's simple and explicit, and it suits read-heavy workloads well.

## Key Design
Cache keys should be deterministic and include:
- Endpoint path
- Normalized query parameters
- API version
- Relevant request context, such as locale

For example:  
`v1:products:list:category=books:page=2:locale=en-US`

## Expiration and Invalidation
Each cached item gets a TTL based on how often that endpoint's data changes:
- Reference data: 1–24 hours
- Frequently updated entities: 1–5 minutes
- Aggregated results: 30–120 seconds

Writes that affect cached resources should trigger invalidation. If a product is updated, for instance, the related product detail and listing keys should be deleted or versioned. When exact invalidation is hard to get right, we should fall back on shorter TTLs.

## Reliability Considerations
To prevent cache stampedes, the system should support either request coalescing or a soft TTL with background refresh. We could also use negative caching for a short time on known missing resources, which cuts down on repeated misses. If the cache goes down, the API must fall back gracefully to the backend.

## Security
Sensitive data shouldn't be cached unless it's encrypted and scoped per user. By default, public and shared caches must leave out authenticated or personalized responses.

## Observability
We should track:
- Cache hit rate
- Miss rate
- Eviction rate
- Latency by endpoint
- Reduction in backend requests

We should also add structured logs and dashboards so we can see whether the cache is actually working.

## Rollout Plan
We'd begin with a small set of GET endpoints that are read heavily and don't change much. Once we've measured hit rate and latency improvements, we expand gradually. Rolling out in phases keeps risk low while we confirm the real-world impact.

**Library of Alexandria**

The **Library of Alexandria** was among the most famous libraries of the ancient world, and during the **Hellenistic period** it was a major center of scholarship in **Alexandria**, Egypt. It was tied to the **Mouseion** ("Temple of the Muses"), a research institution the **Ptolemaic dynasty** set up after the conquests of **Alexander the Great**. A lot about it is still uncertain, but the library has become a symbol of learning, intellectual ambition, and cultural loss.

It was probably founded in the early 3rd century BCE, most likely under **Ptolemy I Soter** or his son **Ptolemy II Philadelphus**. The Ptolemies wanted Alexandria to be the leading center of Greek culture and scholarship, so they collected texts from all over the Mediterranean world: literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, and history. Ancient sources describe an aggressive acquisition policy. Books that arrived in the city were reportedly copied, and sometimes the library kept the originals and sent the copies back to their owners.

The library wasn't just a place to store scrolls. It was part of a larger scholarly community. Scholars who lived and worked there studied, edited, and compared texts, and they helped produce critical editions of major Greek authors such as **Homer**. The institution drew prominent thinkers, among them **Euclid**, **Eratosthenes**, **Aristarchus of Samothrace**, and **Callimachus**. Tradition credits Callimachus with compiling the **Pinakes**, a huge bibliographic catalogue that is often considered one of the earliest library catalogues in history.

Estimates of how big the library was differ a great deal. Ancient and modern figures run from tens of thousands to several hundred thousand scrolls. Scholars also still debate exactly how the library was organized, and how the main library related to a possible "daughter library" in the **Serapeum**.

The destruction of the library is one of the best-known episodes in cultural history, though it probably didn't happen in one catastrophic event. Ancient and later sources link its decline to several episodes: **Julius Caesar's** campaign in Alexandria in 48 BCE, political turmoil during the Roman period, and the destruction of pagan institutions in late antiquity, especially in the 4th century CE. Modern historians generally conclude that the library shrank gradually over centuries and was not suddenly wiped out.

Its legacy has lasted far beyond antiquity. It has come to stand for the ideal of universal knowledge and for how fragile cultural memory is. In modern Alexandria, the **Bibliotheca Alexandrina**, inaugurated in 2002, was conceived as a tribute to the ancient institution and its lasting place in world history.

# Hanseatic League

The **Hanseatic League**, also called the **Hansa**, was a commercial and defensive confederation of merchant guilds and market towns in Northern and Central Europe. It began in the 12th century and peaked between the 13th and 15th centuries, when it dominated trade across the Baltic Sea and North Sea regions. Most of its member cities lay along the coasts of what is now Germany, Poland, the Baltic states, and neighboring regions.

## Origins

The League grew out of associations of German merchants who traveled together to protect themselves from pirates and bandits. Lübeck was founded in 1143 and became a gateway to the Baltic, which was central to this development. Its alliance with Hamburg, set out in the 1241 agreement, is often cited as an early milestone. Over time many other towns signed on, among them Cologne, Bremen, Danzig (Gdańsk), Riga, and Tallinn (Reval).

## Organization

The Hansa was never a state in the modern sense. It had no standing army, no permanent treasury, and no formal constitution. It was a loose association run through periodic assemblies called the *Hansetag*, which met mostly in Lübeck. Decisions were enforced through collective economic pressure, such as trade embargoes, and sometimes through military action. Lübeck is generally seen as the League's leading city and is often called its "Queen."

## Trade

Hanseatic merchants dealt in bulk goods. From the east they carried timber, furs, wax, amber, grain, and rye. From the west and south they brought back cloth, wine, and manufactured goods. Salted herring from Scania and salt from Lüneburg were also vital. The League kept key overseas trading posts, known as *Kontore*, in London (the Steelyard), Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod (the Peterhof). These enclaves had special privileges and ran under their own rules.

## Conflicts

The Hansa's power put it at odds with rulers who resented its trading privileges. The most significant clash was a war with Denmark, which ended with the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370 and confirmed Hanseatic dominance in the Baltic. Later, competition from Dutch, English, and Scandinavian merchants steadily wore down its position.

## Decline

From the late 15th century the League grew weaker, for several reasons: strong territorial states were rising, trade routes were shifting toward the Atlantic, Dutch commercial power was growing, and the members were divided among themselves. Losing key privileges hurt further, as when the Steelyard in London was closed in 1598. The last formal assembly met in 1669, though Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen kept the Hanseatic name for centuries afterward.

## Legacy

The League left a lasting architectural and cultural mark, especially the brick Gothic buildings found across the Baltic. Hamburg and Bremen still carry "Free and Hanseatic City" in their official titles. Today the "New Hanse" and the annual Hanseatic Days celebrate this heritage.
