The **Dust Bowl** was a stretch of brutal dust storms and ecological catastrophe that hit the Great Plains of the United States in the 1930s, with the worst of it coming between 1934 and 1936. Three things combined to cause it: a long drought, high winds, and farming practices that left the soil open to erosion. The damage was environmental, economic, and social, and it fell especially hard on Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico.

Before all this, deep-rooted native grasses covered much of the Great Plains and kept the soil anchored. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, though, huge stretches of prairie were plowed up for wheat and cattle grazing. Crop prices were high, and plenty of people believed that "rain follows the plow," so farmers pushed into marginal land. Then the drought arrived in the early 1930s. The bare topsoil dried out, and strong winds lifted it with little effort.

The dust storms became the most visible sign of the era. People called them "black blizzards," and they carried enormous clouds of soil over towns, farms, and even cities far away. One of the most famous hit on April 14, 1935, remembered as **Black Sunday**, when a massive wall of dust rolled across the southern Plains. The storms ruined crops, buried machinery, and killed livestock. They also contributed to widespread respiratory illness known as "dust pneumonia."

The Dust Bowl made the **Great Depression** even harder to bear. Farm incomes collapsed, banks failed, and many families lost their land. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, especially from Oklahoma and Arkansas, heading for California and other western states in search of work and a better life. They were often called "Okies," even though many came from other states. John Steinbeck's *The Grapes of Wrath* later portrayed their experiences.

Under President Franklin D. Roosevelt's **New Deal**, the federal government responded with a mix of conservation and relief measures. In 1935 it created the Soil Conservation Service, which promoted ways of farming that cut down on erosion, such as contour plowing, crop rotation, strip farming, and planting shelterbelts of trees. Assistance programs also helped struggling farm families either relocate or stay on their land.

Rain gradually came back to the Plains in the late 1930s, and the worst conditions eased. The Dust Bowl is still regarded as one of the most significant environmental disasters in U.S. history. People often point to it as a warning about unsustainable land use, climate extremes, and how vulnerable agricultural systems are to ecological change.

# The Friendship That Lives in My Pocket

When I was twelve, my best friend moved across the country and we started writing letters. They were messy things, with words crossed out and little drawings in the margins. A reply took two weeks, sometimes three. I still remember the jolt of seeing her handwriting in the mailbox, and I read every letter so many times that the folds went soft. Within a year we'd lost touch. That's just what distance did back then.

My kids will never lose someone that way, and I honestly haven't figured out how I feel about that.

I notice how much social media has changed friendship whenever I try to explain it to someone. I know what my college roommate ate for dinner last night. I know her daughter lost a tooth, that her mother has been sick, that she's fed up with her job. I haven't actually talked to her in four years. Is she my friend? By the old definition, probably not. These days she's someone I "keep up with," which is a weird category when you think about it: closeness without contact, intimacy where nobody exchanges anything.

I don't want to pretend it's all bad. I've seen friendships make it through moves, career changes, and the ordinary drifting apart that used to finish them off. One friend lives in another time zone and sends me voice memos while she walks her dog. I answer while I'm doing the dishes. It isn't the same as sitting across a table from her, but it isn't nothing either. It's a thread, and a thread can be pulled tight again. When we do see each other, we aren't starting from zero.

The downsides are quieter, though, and I've felt them more as I've gotten older. Social media turns friendship into something you perform for an audience. I've caught myself putting a moment together while I'm still in it, turning the dinner table to get a better photo, working out a caption while a friend is halfway through a sentence. The evening becomes content, and my friend becomes a co-star, just a little.

It's also made affection cheap. A like costs nothing. A birthday message prompted by a platform's reminder takes about four seconds. We send these little tokens and feel like we've done the work of caring, but real friendship has always asked for something less efficient: showing up, sitting through awkward silences, driving across town when someone's life falls apart. No app has automated that, even if it has made us feel like we don't have to.

Last winter a friend I'd only ever "liked" from a distance posted something vague and sad. I almost scrolled right past it. Instead I called her. We talked for two hours, and she cried, and I realized how long it had been since I'd heard her real voice. The post was a small flare, and I'd nearly taken it for scenery.

So that's where I've ended up. Social media didn't ruin friendship, and it didn't perfect it either. It widened the net and thinned the rope. What we do with the slack is up to us: we can treat the feed as the friendship itself, or as a doorway into one.

I still have my friend's old letters, soft at the folds. I don't want to go back to waiting three weeks for a reply. But I'd like to write like that again, slowly, with crossed-out words, meaning every one.

By Thursday afternoon, something odd happens in my office. People are still answering emails, sitting in meetings, and updating spreadsheets, but the energy is different. Monday's sharpness is gone. Conversations wander. Small tasks drag. By Friday it can feel like we're all performing work more than doing it. That feeling has made me more and more sympathetic to the idea of a four-day work week.

It isn't the prospect of one more day to sleep in that persuades me, though I won't pretend that doesn't appeal. It's the growing sense that more time at work doesn't always mean better work. In plenty of jobs, especially office jobs, productivity isn't just a matter of hours logged. Attention is limited. Creativity wears out when it's overused. Tired people make sloppier decisions. We talk as though endurance were the highest professional virtue, but in practice clarity matters more than sheer duration. A shorter week admits something deeply human: people aren't machines, and acting as if they are usually produces mediocrity.

I also like that a four-day week treats rest as something valuable instead of indulgent. In many workplaces, exhaustion is worn like a badge of honor. If you're overwhelmed, you must be important; if you're unreachable, you must be needed. That logic feels more hollow to me all the time. Rest isn't the opposite of responsibility. It's one of the conditions that makes responsibility possible. An extra day off can mean time to recover, to care for children or parents, to book a doctor's appointment without stress, to read, to exercise, to exist outside the demands of employers and inboxes. When people have room for fuller lives, they often come back to work more focused and less resentful.

I think there's a moral argument here too. For generations, technological advances have been sold to us as routes to efficiency and freedom. Yet for many workers, those efficiencies haven't turned into more leisure, just higher expectations. We can reply to messages instantly, produce documents faster, and automate routine tasks, and the reward is often simply more work. A four-day week suggests another possibility: that the benefits of innovation could finally be shared as time. Time is, after all, one of the most precious things anyone has.

Of course, not every profession can adopt the same schedule in the same way. Hospitals, schools, factories, and service industries all face practical constraints. A four-day week won't magically fix every workplace problem. It takes careful implementation, staffing adjustments, and a real commitment not to cram five days of meetings into four. But the existence of challenges doesn't weaken the central idea. If anything, it makes the case for rethinking old assumptions stronger.

For me, the case for a four-day work week is ultimately a case for dignity. It asks whether work should consume the best of our lives or support them. I don't think people want to contribute less. I think they want to contribute sustainably, and still have enough of themselves left for the rest of life.

# Wildfire Forces Thousands to Evacuate Near Cedar Ridge National Park

**CEDAR FALLS, Mont.** — A wildfire raced through dry timber on the western edge of Cedar Ridge National Park on Tuesday. More than 3,000 residents were forced to evacuate, and officials closed the park to all visitors.

The Hollow Creek Fire was first reported shortly after 2 p.m. Monday. It has since burned an estimated 14,000 acres, and as of Wednesday morning fire officials said it was zero percent contained.

"This fire is moving faster than anything we've seen in this area in a decade," Incident Commander Dana Whitfield said at an evening briefing. "Dry fuels, low humidity, and gusting winds are all working against us."

Mandatory evacuation orders went out for Pine Hollow, Larkspur, and parts of Cedar Falls. Another 2,000 residents in nearby areas were told to be ready to leave on short notice. Sheriff's deputies went door to door overnight, and emergency alerts were sent to cell phones across the county.

The Red Cross set up an evacuation center at Cedar Falls High School, offering cots, meals, and information. By midday more than 400 people had checked in, many of them carrying pets and medications and not much else.

"We had about fifteen minutes to grab what we could," said Maria Delgado, who lives in Larkspur and left with her two children and their dog. "I took photo albums, documents, and clothes. You just hope the house is still there when you get back."

Park Superintendent Tom Ellery said all campgrounds and trails have been cleared, and rangers have accounted for every registered backcountry visitor. "Visitor safety is our top priority," he said. "We are also working closely with firefighters to protect historic structures, including the Ridgeline Lodge, which dates to 1932."

More than 600 firefighters are fighting the fire, backed by helicopters and air tankers. Crews have concentrated on building containment lines near homes and protecting power infrastructure. Two firefighters had minor heat-related injuries, officials said. No civilian injuries or deaths have been reported.

Smoke has spread across the region, and health officials issued air quality warnings for three counties. They urged children, older adults, and anyone with respiratory conditions to stay indoors.

Meteorologists said there's a slight chance of rain late Friday. Any thunderstorms, though, could bring dangerous lightning and erratic winds.

Governor Elaine Parks declared a state of emergency Tuesday, which frees up more state resources. The cause of the fire hasn't been determined, and an investigation is underway.

Updates and shelter information are available on the county emergency management website.

# The Weight of Boxes

What I noticed first about the new city was how loud the quiet was. In my old apartment I knew every noise: the radiator knocking, the upstairs neighbor stomping around, the bus groaning past at 6:40 every morning. In the sublet, which smelled a little like someone else's dinner, I lay awake trying to work out what I was hearing.

People don't tell you that moving is a bit like choosing to forget things. You give up being fluent. I'd lived in my old city for nine years and could get around it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had decent tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order as soon as I walked in. Here I got lost on the way to the pharmacy. I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, totally thrown by brands I'd never seen. It was humbling, and kind of ridiculous, to feel like a kid at thirty-four.

But the humbling turned out to be a gift too. Within a week I was paying attention in a way I hadn't for years. I noticed the brick on my street, a warm rusty color that glowed at dusk. I noticed that people here nodded at strangers. I took the long way everywhere, since I didn't have a short way yet. A city you don't know makes you look at it, and I realized I'd stopped letting myself enjoy looking. Routine had been sanding my days down until they all felt the same.

There were smaller pleasures, too. I found a bakery where the owner started saving me the end pieces of the rye loaf. # The Weight of Boxes

What I noticed first about the new city was how loud the quiet was. In my old apartment I knew every noise: the radiator knocking, the upstairs neighbor stomping around, the bus groaning past at 6:40 every morning. In the sublet, which smelled a little like someone else's dinner, I lay awake trying to work out what I was hearing.

People don't tell you that moving is a bit like choosing to forget things. You give up being fluent. I'd lived in my old city for nine years and could get around it half asleep. I knew which grocery store had decent tomatoes, which streets flooded in spring, which barista would start my order as soon as I walked in. Here I got lost on the way to the pharmacy. I stood in the cereal aisle for ten minutes, totally thrown by brands I'd never seen. It was humbling, and kind of ridiculous, to feel like a kid at thirty-four.

# Dust Bowl

The **Dust Bowl**, sometimes called the **Dirty Thirties**, was a stretch of severe dust storms in the 1930s that did major ecological and agricultural damage to the prairie lands of the United States and Canada. Two things combined to cause it: a severe drought, and decades of heavy farming that skipped the techniques that guard against wind erosion, like crop rotation, cover crops, and terracing.

## Background

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, settlers poured onto the Great Plains. The Homestead Acts encouraged them, and so did unusually wet weather in the early 1900s. They plowed under the native deep-rooted prairie grasses to plant wheat. Wheat prices were high during and after World War I, which sped up the expansion, and gasoline-powered tractors and combines meant farmers could work far more land than ever before. Millions of acres of grassland became cropland, and the soil was left exposed.

## Drought and storms

Drought set in around 1930 and came back in waves through 1936 and again in 1939–1940. The grasses that had once held the soil in place were gone, so high winds picked up the dry topsoil and whipped it into huge clouds. The hardest-hit area took in the panhandles of Texas and Oklahoma, plus parts of western Kansas, eastern Colorado, and northeastern New Mexico.

On **April 14, 1935**, a day remembered as "Black Sunday," a massive storm swept dust across the southern plains and turned day into night. The next day, journalist Robert Geiger used the term "Dust Bowl" in a news dispatch, and the name stuck. Some storms carried dust as far as Washington, D.C., and out to ships in the Atlantic Ocean.

## Human impact

The storms ruined crops, buried farm equipment, and killed livestock. Many residents came down with "dust pneumonia" and other respiratory illnesses. On top of the economic hardship of the Great Depression, all this forced many families off their farms. About 3.5 million people left the Plains states in the 1930s, and many of them headed for California. Their stories were recorded in John Steinbeck's novel *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939), Dorothea Lange's photographs, and Woody Guthrie's songs.

## Government response

The federal government set up programs to deal with the crisis. The Soil Conservation Service, created in 1935 and led by Hugh Hammond Bennett, pushed soil-saving methods such as contour plowing, strip cropping, and crop rotation. The Prairie States Forestry Project, which began in 1934, planted millions of trees across the Plains as windbreaks known as shelterbelts. The Taylor Grazing Act of 1934 also put rules on grazing on public lands.

## Legacy

Rain returned in late 1939 and the drought ended. The Dust Bowl is still counted among the worst environmental disasters in American history, and it shaped modern soil conservation policy and farming practices.

The Erie Canal is one of New York State's best-known historic landmarks, and it did a great deal to shape the American economy in the 19th century. It opened in 1825 and gave boats a continuous water route from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo, connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Great Lakes. Shipping got much cheaper, settlers moved west faster, and New York City became the country's leading port.

The idea came up in the early 1800s, when moving goods and people across the Appalachian barrier was a real problem. Travel over land was slow, expensive, and often unreliable. Governor DeWitt Clinton became the project's strongest political champion, and critics mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch." Work began in 1817. Thousands of laborers, many of them immigrants, cleared forests, dug trenches, and built aqueducts and locks across difficult terrain.

When it was finished, the original canal ran about 363 miles (584 km), was 40 feet (12 m) wide, and was 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. Its 83 locks let boats climb a total elevation difference of more than 500 feet (150 m) between the Hudson River and Lake Erie. The official opening came on October 26, 1825. To mark it, Clinton staged the "Wedding of the Waters," a ceremonial trip from Buffalo to New York Harbor in which water from Lake Erie was poured into the Atlantic Ocean.

The canal soon became one of the most important transportation routes in North America. Freight rates between the Midwest and the East Coast dropped sharply, so shipping farm products, raw materials, and manufactured goods cost much less. Towns and cities along the way, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew quickly. It also drew people to western New York, Ohio, Indiana, and other parts of the Old Northwest.

Since it worked so well, the canal was enlarged several times over the 19th century. In the early 20th century, much of the original route was folded into the larger New York State Barge Canal System, which opened in 1918 and used both canalized rivers and new canal cuts. Railroads and highways eventually cut into its commercial importance, but the Erie Canal remained a symbol of American engineering and ambition.

These days the canal is used mostly for recreation, tourism, and heritage purposes. People celebrate it as a landmark in the history of transportation, commerce, and the expansion of the United States.

Picking up a second language as an adult taught me that intelligence is a much humbler thing than I used to think. Before I started, I saw language learning as a test of memory, discipline, and maybe talent. I figured that if I worked hard enough I'd climb steadily from confusion to fluency, gathering grammar rules and vocabulary the way you gather tools. It didn't go like that. It felt more like learning how to be a beginner again.

When I was a kid, I never noticed how much of life runs on language. I moved through my first one without thinking. I joked, apologized, complained, and told stories as easily as I breathed. Then I started learning another language as an adult, and even the simplest exchanges felt strangely heavy. A thought could be in full color in my head, and I'd find I only had the words to express it in black and white. The person I thought of as articulate and quick turned hesitant and simple in the new language. It was startling to see how much of what I called "myself" depended on being able to express it easily.

It made me more patient, and not just with myself. Once you've struggled to ask where the bathroom is, or ordered the wrong food by accident, or misunderstood a question and answered it confidently anyway, you get more generous about how people communicate. I started to notice how brave people are every day when they live, work, and raise families in a language that isn't fully theirs. Before, I admired bilingualism in an abstract way. Afterward, I saw it as a kind of daily courage.

It also taught me that embarrassment is survivable. Adults tend to avoid anything that makes them look foolish. Kids don't get a choice. They're corrected, misunderstood, and exposed all the time, and they keep going. Adults guard their competence as if it were fragile. Learning another language made me speak badly, mispronounce things, forget words I'd "already learned," and hear the limits of my own mouth and memory. At first that was frustrating. Eventually it felt freeing. I realized that getting better has less to do with avoiding mistakes than with putting up with them.

Maybe the most unexpected change was in how I listened. In my native language I often listen for meaning alone, but in a second language I listen for structure, tone, rhythm, and intention. I notice what's said, what's implied, and what I might have missed. That kind of listening started following me into my first language too. I got slower to assume and quicker to ask, and more aware that understanding another person is never as automatic as it seems.

Learning a second language as an adult didn't just give me another way to speak. It changed how I think about fluency, identity, and patience. It taught me that growth is often awkward, that humility can be useful, and that communication is both more fragile and more generous than I used to know. More than anything, it reminded me that becoming a beginner again isn't a return to weakness. It's a return to attention.

**Record Turnout Marks Local School-Board Election**

Riverton voters showed up in record numbers Tuesday for the school board election, a race that usually draws little notice outside education circles.

The Riverton County Elections Office said more than 18,400 ballots were cast, or roughly 46 percent of registered voters in the district. That's the highest turnout ever for a stand-alone school-board election in the community. It beat the old mark, set in 2017, by nearly 5,000 votes.

Election workers said lines stayed steady all day at polling sites across the district, and were especially heavy in the morning and again after work. Early voting and absentee ballots also jumped sharply, which helped push participation to an unprecedented level.

"This is the kind of civic engagement every local government hopes to see," said County Elections Director Marisol Vega. "School-board elections typically bring in a smaller slice of the electorate, so this level of turnout is remarkable."

The surge followed months of public debate over school funding, classroom overcrowding, campus safety, and where the district's curriculum is headed. Candidate forums drew big crowds, and community groups on every side ran extensive outreach campaigns urging people to vote.

Three seats were open. Incumbent Daniel Harper kept his, and newcomers Alicia Gomez and Trent Wallace appeared headed for wins based on unofficial returns released Tuesday night. Final certified results are expected later this week. The margins were wide enough, observers said, that the outcome is unlikely to change.

Supporters of the winners celebrated what they called a clear message from voters: the district needs both stability and fresh ideas. "People care deeply about what happens in our schools," Gomez told supporters at a gathering Tuesday evening. "Tonight's turnout shows this community is paying attention and wants a voice in the decisions affecting students and families."

Not everyone read the results the same way, but many residents said the sheer number of voters was encouraging. Parents, teachers, and retirees interviewed outside polling sites said they believe the school board has an outsized effect on daily life, from academic standards to bus routes and extracurricular programs.

Superintendent Karen Liu said the election showed broad public investment in the district's future. "Regardless of who people supported, it is heartening to see so many residents participate," Liu said. "That kind of involvement strengthens public education."

Local analysts said the turnout could change how future elections play out, since it shows school-board races can mobilize voters when the issues feel immediate and personal. For Riverton, Tuesday brought new leadership and a notable show of democratic engagement.

**Startup Recalls Faulty Home Battery After Overheating Reports**

VoltNest Energy, a fast-growing home energy startup, has voluntarily recalled one of its residential battery systems. Reports say a defect can make the unit overheat, which raises the risk of fire in homes where it's installed.

The company said Tuesday that it is recalling about **8,200 units** of the **PowerVault S1**, a wall-mounted battery that stores electricity from rooftop solar panels or provides backup power during outages. The batteries were sold in the United States between **March 2024 and September 2026** through solar installers and VoltNest's website.

VoltNest said it has received **27 reports of overheating**. Five of those involved **minor property damage**, such as scorched walls and melted wiring insulation. No serious injuries have been reported, though two customers sought medical evaluation for possible smoke inhalation.

The company believes the problem comes from a manufacturing defect in a batch of lithium iron phosphate battery modules from a third-party vendor. Under certain charging conditions, it said, an internal component can fail and potentially cause excessive heat buildup.

"We are acting out of an abundance of caution," VoltNest Chief Executive Maya Levin said in the statement. "Customer safety is our top priority, and we are working closely with regulators, installers and homeowners to replace affected units as quickly as possible."

Customers should **shut down the battery immediately** with the system's main disconnect switch, and they shouldn't try to repair or remove it themselves. VoltNest said it will provide **free inspections, software diagnostics and unit replacements** where necessary. It has also released a firmware update meant to reduce charging stress until replacements are carried out, but it stressed that the patch is **not a substitute for the recall**.

The recall was announced in coordination with the **U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission**, which urged owners to follow the shutdown instructions and to contact VoltNest or their installer. The agency said recalled units have serial numbers beginning with **PVS1-24** or **PVS1-25**.

The recall is a major test for VoltNest, a venture-backed startup that has pitched itself as a lower-cost rival in the booming home battery market. Founded in 2021, it has grown quickly as demand for residential backup power rises amid more frequent extreme weather and strained electric grids.

Industry analysts said the recall could temporarily slow the company's momentum, but that how VoltNest handles the response may matter more than the defect itself.

"Recalls are damaging, especially for a young brand," said energy storage analyst Daniel Cho. "But in this industry, transparency and speed matter. Homeowners need confidence that these systems are safe inside their garages and utility rooms."

# Svalbard Global Seed Vault

The **Svalbard Global Seed Vault** (Norwegian: *Svalbard globale frøhvelv*) is a secure backup facility for the world's crop diversity. It sits on the Norwegian island of Spitsbergen in the Svalbard archipelago, and the media often call it the "Doomsday Vault." It holds duplicate samples of seeds kept in gene banks around the world, so that collections lost to accident, mismanagement, war, or natural disaster can be replaced.

## History

People first proposed the vault in the 1980s, and it picked up momentum thanks to the work of agricultural scientist Cary Fowler, who later headed the Global Crop Diversity Trust (now the Crop Trust). The Norwegian government paid for construction, which came to roughly NOK 50 million. The facility opened on 26 February 2008.

## Location and design

The vault is cut into a sandstone mountain near Longyearbyen, about 1,300 kilometres from the North Pole and roughly 130 metres above sea level. That height was picked to keep it above any projected rise in sea level. A tunnel about 120 metres long leads to three storage chambers, each built to hold up to 1.5 million seed samples. Altogether the vault can hold 4.5 million varieties, or about 2.25 billion seeds.

The permafrost around it cools the chambers naturally, and refrigeration holds them at about −18 °C, the standard temperature for long-term seed storage. At that temperature, and with low moisture, the seeds of many major crops can stay viable for centuries or even longer. The site was also chosen because it is geologically stable and has little tectonic activity.

## Operation

The Norwegian government owns the vault and manages it together with the Crop Trust and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen). Storage costs depositors nothing, since Norway and the Crop Trust cover the expenses. Institutions that deposit seeds keep ownership of them. The samples are sealed in foil packages and placed in boxes that nobody else is allowed to open. The vault serves purely as a backup, and only the depositors can withdraw their material.

By the early 2020s the collection held more than 1.2 million samples from nearly every country. They include varieties of rice, wheat, maize, barley, sorghum, and many regional crops.

## Notable events

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first major withdrawal. The Syrian civil war had disrupted the operations of its gene bank, and the center asked for copies of seeds originally held in Aleppo, Syria. It used them to re-establish collections in Morocco and Lebanon.

In 2017, unusually warm weather and heavy rain sent meltwater into the entrance tunnel. The seeds were unaffected, but Norway went on to fund substantial upgrades, including waterproofing and improved drainage.

## Significance

The vault stands as a symbol of international cooperation on food security and biodiversity conservation. It also shows that climate change can threaten even facilities designed to withstand long-term risks.

Altogether the vault can hold 4.5 million varieties, or about 2.25 billion seeds.

The permafrost around it cools the chambers naturally, and refrigeration holds them at about −18 °C, the standard temperature for long-term seed storage. At that temperature, and with low moisture, the seeds of many major crops can stay viable for centuries or even longer. The site was also chosen because it is geologically stable and has little tectonic activity.

## Operation

The Norwegian government owns the vault and manages it together with the Crop Trust and the Nordic Genetic Resource Center (NordGen). Storage costs depositors nothing, since Norway and the Crop Trust cover the expenses. Institutions that deposit seeds keep ownership of them. The samples are sealed in foil packages and placed in boxes that nobody else is allowed to open. The vault serves purely as a backup, and only the depositors can withdraw their material.

By the early 2020s the collection held more than 1.2 million samples from nearly every country. They include varieties of rice, wheat, maize, barley, sorghum, and many regional crops.

## Notable events

In 2015, the International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) made the first major withdrawal. The Syrian civil war had disrupted the operations of its gene bank, and the center asked for copies of seeds originally held in Aleppo, Syria. It used them to re-establish collections in Morocco and Lebanon.

In 2017, unusually warm weather and heavy rain sent meltwater into the entrance tunnel. The seeds were unaffected, but Norway went on to fund substantial upgrades, including waterproofing and improved drainage.

## Significance

The vault stands as a symbol of international cooperation on food security and biodiversity conservation. It also shows that climate change can threaten even facilities designed to withstand long-term risks.

I've never trusted a habit that comes with a lot of ceremony. The ones that actually save me are small, almost shy: making coffee before I'm fully awake, opening a window even in winter, going for a walk for no particular reason. Walking is the one I lean on most. It asks the least of me and gives back the most.

I didn't always think of it as a practice. For a long time it was just what happened between places: errands, late buses, parking two streets away, crossing campus in bad weather. It was practical and forgettable, and often a little annoying. At some point, though, it changed categories. It stopped being a delay before my life started and became a way of getting into it.

Part of the comfort is how undramatic it is. You don't need talent or special equipment or the right mood, and it doesn't ask me to improve myself. When I'm tired or restless or vaguely discontented in that modern way, with too much screen and too many tabs open in my head, I can still put on my shoes and go outside. That simplicity feels almost like a correction. So much of life now is frictionless in all the wrong ways. Messages arrive instantly, the news follows me from room to room, and whole afternoons disappear while my body sits still. Walking brings back a useful kind of friction. It reminds me that distance is real, weather is real, and my legs are real.

My thoughts act differently when I'm walking. At a desk, problems tend to harden into something dense and airless, like a thing I've handled too much. Out on a walk, even familiar worries loosen up. The rhythm of my steps gives my mind just enough to do that it stops gripping so tightly. I've had ideas show up while crossing intersections. I've remembered lines I thought I'd lost, and I've forgiven people a little, and myself a little too. None of this feels mystical to me. Movement just changes the scale of thought. What seemed inescapable indoors turns into one thing among many: a barking dog, a passing train, the smell of cut grass, the sudden authority of a tree.

Walking also gets me back into my senses, in a very literal way. The world stops being a backdrop and starts feeling like company. The same street is never quite the same street. It gets revised with the seasons: wet leaves plastered to the sidewalk, the medicinal brightness of cold air, the worn-out abundance of late summer gardens. And there are small neighborhood dramas, like a child chalking suns on the pavement, someone learning to ride a bike, a curtain lifted and dropped. If you walk regularly, you become a modest sort of witness. You learn what the dogs are like, when the sprinklers go on, and where the first crocuses insist on coming up. Familiarity piles up, and a quiet affection comes with it.

What I value most, though, is that walking is a kind of progress you can't optimize into meaninglessness. One foot in front of the other is both an instruction and a philosophy. You don't have to leap, and you don't have to finish everything today. You move, you pause, you keep going. There's humility in that, and relief.

When I get back from a walk, my life is usually unchanged in any way you could measure. The emails are still there, and so are the unanswered questions. But I feel slightly rejoined to myself. I've been reminded that the world is bigger than my preoccupations, and that I can meet it with my own body, at a human pace. For such an ordinary habit, walking has an astonishing power: it brings me back to proportion. More and more, that feels like a form of grace.

## Create Calendar Event

Use this endpoint to add a new event to a user's calendar.

### Endpoint

`POST /v1/events`

### Description

To create an event, send a title, a start time, and an end time. You can also include a description, location, attendees, reminders, recurrence, and time zone if you want them. If the request succeeds, the API gives you back the new event object, which includes its unique identifier.

### Authentication

You'll need a valid bearer token:

```http
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
```

### Request Headers

| Header | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| Authorization | string | Yes | Bearer access token |
| Content-Type | string | Yes | Must be `application/json` |

### Request Body

```json
{
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "reminders": [
    {
      "method": "email",
      "minutesBefore": 30
    }
  ],
  "recurrence": {
    "frequency": "weekly",
    "interval": 1
  }
}
```

### Body Parameters

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| title | string | Yes | Event title, max 200 characters |
| start | string | Yes | Start date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| end | string | Yes | End date/time in ISO 8601 format |
| description | string | No | Event details, max 5000 characters |
| location | string | No | Event location |
| timezone | string | No | IANA time zone, e.g. `America/New_York` |
| attendees | array[string] | No | List of attendee email addresses |
| reminders | array[object] | No | Reminder definitions |
| reminders[].method | string | Yes | `email` or `popup` |
| reminders[].minutesBefore | integer | Yes | Minutes before event start |
| recurrence | object | No | Recurrence settings |
| recurrence.frequency | string | No | `daily`, `weekly`, `monthly`, or `yearly` |
| recurrence.interval | integer | No | Repeat interval, must be greater than 0 |

### Response

**201 Created**

```json
{
  "id": "evt_01J9X8K7M2R4A6P9",
  "title": "Team Sync",
  "start": "2026-11-20T09:00:00Z",
  "end": "2026-11-20T09:30:00Z",
  "description": "Weekly project status meeting",
  "location": "Conference Room A",
  "timezone": "UTC",
  "attendees": [
    "alex@example.com",
    "sam@example.com"
  ],
  "status": "confirmed",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-10T14:22:31Z"
}
```

### Error Responses

| Status | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| 400 Bad Request | Required fields are missing, the JSON is invalid, or the dates are malformed |
| 401 Unauthorized | The access token is missing or invalid |
| 403 Forbidden | The token doesn't have permission to create events |
| 409 Conflict | The event overlaps with a protected calendar block |
| 422 Unprocessable Entity | Validation failed, for example because `end` comes before `start` |

Example error:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "validation_error",
    "message": "The `end` time must be later than `start`."
  }
}
```

### Notes

- Every timestamp must be in ISO 8601 format.
- If you leave out `timezone`, the calendar's default time zone is used.
- Depending on account settings, attendees may get invitations.
- A recurring event may create a whole series instead of a single standalone event.

# Cyberattack at Riverbend Health Exposes Records of Nearly 380,000 Patients

**Hospital network says names, Social Security numbers and treatment details were accessed; investigators believe attackers were inside systems for three weeks**

*RIVERBEND, Ohio* — Attackers broke into the systems of Riverbend Health and may have stolen personal and medical information on about 378,000 current and former patients, the company confirmed Tuesday. Riverbend is a regional network of seven hospitals and more than 40 outpatient clinics.

In a statement on its website, the network said IT staff noticed odd data transfers from a server that stores billing records, and that's how they found the suspicious activity on March 4. It believes the intruders had been in the system since mid-February.

"We deeply regret this incident and the concern it causes our patients," said Dr. Elaine Marchetti, Riverbend Health's chief executive. "Protecting patient information is central to our mission, and we are taking every step to understand what happened and prevent it from happening again."

The network said the affected data may include names, birth dates, home addresses, Social Security numbers, insurance information, and details of diagnoses and treatments. It said it has found no evidence that the attackers got into its electronic health record system, where full clinical charts are kept, but added that the investigation is still going.

Emergency departments stayed open throughout. Still, the network confirmed that some scheduling and billing systems were offline for almost a week, and several patients said their appointments were rescheduled and their test results delayed.

"I showed up for a follow-up and they were writing everything on paper," said Dana Whitfield, 54, who is treated at a Riverbend cardiology clinic. "Now I'm worried about who has my information."

Riverbend has brought in an outside cybersecurity firm and notified the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which keeps a public list of large healthcare breaches. The network said no ransom demand has come in. However, a ransomware group has claimed responsibility on a dark web leak site and posted what it says are sample files. Riverbend said it is looking into those claims.

Security experts note that healthcare organizations are still prime targets, since medical records hold a rich mix of data that can fuel identity theft and fraud.

"A stolen credit card can be canceled in minutes. A Social Security number and medical history can be exploited for years," said Raymond Okafor, a health care cybersecurity consultant who is not involved in the investigation.

Notification letters will start going out next week, and Riverbend is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity theft protection. Patients can reach a dedicated hotline at 1-800-555-0142.

The network advised patients to check their insurance statements for services they don't recognize and to consider placing fraud alerts on their credit files.

*Note: This article is a fictional work created for illustrative purposes.*

# Antikythera mechanism

The **Antikythera mechanism** is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, and it's often called the earliest known analog computer. People used it to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades ahead, and to follow the cycles of the Greek calendar, including when the major Panhellenic games were held. It's generally dated to the 2nd or 1st century BCE.

## Discovery

Divers looking for sponges found a Roman-era shipwreck in 1900 off the Greek island of Antikythera, which lies between Kythera and Crete. The following year, salvage operations led by the Greek Navy and archaeologists recovered statues, pottery, jewelry, coins, and a corroded lump of bronze. Only later did anyone realize the lump held gears and inscriptions. Today it's kept at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

## Construction

The mechanism sat inside a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. Its bronze parts, many of them thin and finely cut, survive in 82 known fragments. A crank turned a train of at least 30 interlocking gears with triangular teeth, and these moved pointers across dials on the front and back of the case.

On the front, a dial showed where the Sun and Moon stood in the zodiac, alongside a calendar. A small rotating ball, partly silvered, showed the Moon's phase. The back carried two large spiral dials: one for the Metonic cycle (19 years, which matches solar years to lunar months) and one for the Saros cycle (about 18 years, used to predict eclipses). Smaller dials tracked other cycles, among them the Callippic cycle and the Olympiad cycle.

Because the Moon's orbit is elliptical, its motion is uneven. The mechanism modeled this with a pin-and-slot arrangement that used two gears on offset axes, which reflects the lunar theory attributed to Hipparchus.

## Research

Valerios Stais made early studies, and Derek de Solla Price followed in the 1950s–70s, together establishing what the device basically did. X-ray imaging in the 1970s helped further. Then the Antikythera Mechanism Research Project, which began in 2005, used microfocus X-ray computed tomography and surface imaging to read much of the inscriptions, which amount to a user's manual. Researchers have also suggested that the device showed planetary positions, and reconstructions of that gearing have been published, though the evidence is still incomplete.

## Significance

For more than a thousand years, nothing else that survives matches the mechanism's sophistication, until medieval astronomical clocks appeared in Europe and the Islamic world. Where it came from is debated. Rhodes, Corinth, and Syracuse have all been suggested, as have links to the traditions of Hipparchus or Archimedes. Whatever its origin, it remains a striking demonstration of Hellenistic technology and astronomical knowledge.

# Photo Date Renamer

A small command-line tool that renames your photos after the date they were taken, using their EXIF metadata. Once your files are named by date, they're much easier to sort, search, and archive across folders and devices.

## Features

- Renames photos using the original capture date from the EXIF data
- Works with common image formats like JPG and JPEG
- Keeps filenames consistent and sortable
- Adds a counter when two photos share the same timestamp
- Can handle a single folder or go through subfolders recursively
- Has a dry-run mode so you can preview changes before any files are renamed

## Why use it?

Cameras and phones tend to give you names like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`. These don't tell you much once the files get copied into a bigger collection. This tool swaps them for names based on the timestamp, like these:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

The names are readable and sortable, and they help avoid confusion when you're merging photos from several devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package has been published, you may also be able to install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

To rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

To process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

To preview changes without touching any files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

To use your own filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed with this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos have the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix so nothing gets overwritten.

## Missing metadata

If a file has no valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it by default and mentions it in the summary output. Depending on configuration, future versions may optionally fall back to the file's creation or modification time.

## Safety

- It never overwrites an existing file without warning you
- Dry runs let you preview safely
- At the end of a run, it reports which files were renamed, skipped, or failed

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you find a bug or have a feature idea, please open an issue and include sample filenames, the behavior you expected, and your platform details.

## License

MIT License.

Cameras and phones tend to give you names like `IMG_4032.JPG` or `DSC00123.jpg`. These don't tell you much once the files get copied into a bigger collection. This tool swaps them for names based on the timestamp, like these:

```bash
2023-08-14_18-42-09.jpg
2023-08-14_18-42-09_2.jpg
```

The names are readable and sortable, and they help avoid confusion when you're merging photos from several devices.

## Installation

Clone the repository and install the dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/photo-date-renamer.git
cd photo-date-renamer
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

If the package has been published, you may also be able to install it with:

```bash
pip install photo-date-renamer
```

## Usage

To rename all supported photos in a folder:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos
```

To process folders recursively:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --recursive
```

To preview changes without touching any files:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --dry-run
```

To use your own filename format:

```bash
photo-date-renamer /path/to/photos --format "%Y/%m/%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"
```

## Filename behavior

By default, files are renamed with this pattern:

```text
YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS.ext
```

Examples:

- `IMG_0001.JPG` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21.jpg`
- `DSC7788.jpeg` → `2022-05-06_14-33-21_2.jpeg`

If two or more photos have the same timestamp, the tool adds a numeric suffix so nothing gets overwritten.

## Missing metadata

If a file has no valid capture date in its EXIF metadata, the tool skips it by default and mentions it in the summary output. Depending on configuration, future versions may optionally fall back to the file's creation or modification time.

## Safety

- It never overwrites an existing file without warning you
- Dry runs let you preview safely
- At the end of a run, it reports which files were renamed, skipped, or failed

## Example output

```bash
Renamed: IMG_1203.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-44.jpg
Renamed: IMG_1204.JPG -> 2021-11-03_09-15-45.jpg
Skipped: scan_01.jpg (no EXIF date found)

Done. 2 renamed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
```

## Contributing

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you find a bug or have a feature idea, please open an issue and include sample filenames, the behavior you expected, and your platform details.

**Regional Airline Cancels Dozens of Flights as Pilot Shortage Bites**

A regional airline has scrapped dozens of flights this week, blaming a continuing shortage of qualified pilots. The cancellations have thrown schedules into disarray and sent passengers rushing to find other ways to get where they're going.

The carrier flies short-haul routes linking smaller cities to major hubs. It said the cancellations were needed to keep operations safe and to meet federal crew-rest and staffing requirements. According to airline officials, staffing had dropped below the level needed to run the full schedule reliably.

"We regret the inconvenience to our customers, but safety remains our top priority," the airline said in a statement Tuesday. "Like many regional carriers across the industry, we are facing significant challenges in recruiting and retaining pilots."

Routes in several states were affected, and some passengers found out only hours before departure that their flights were gone. At several regional airports, travelers described long lines at customer service desks while airline staff tried to rebook people on later flights or set up ground transportation.

"I was supposed to fly out this morning for a business meeting, and now the next available flight isn't until tomorrow," one passenger at a regional airport said. "It's frustrating because there weren't many backup options."

Industry analysts say pilot shortages are a growing problem for regional airlines, which often act as a training ground for pilots before they move on to larger, better-paying mainline carriers. Regional carriers have had a hard time competing on pay and quality of life, particularly now that demand for air travel has bounced back and bigger airlines are hiring more.

Mandatory retirement rules, higher training costs, and tougher experience requirements for new pilots have made things worse. Together they have shrunk the pool of available crew, especially for smaller carriers serving less profitable markets.

Aviation consultant Mark Ellison said regional airlines tend to be hit hardest because they have less staffing in reserve. "When a major airline loses a few pilots, it can sometimes absorb that disruption," he said. "For a regional carrier, even a small staffing gap can force widespread cancellations."

The airline said it is offering travel waivers and refunds to affected customers and is working to get back to normal operations as quickly as it can. Company officials added that hiring is underway, including recruitment bonuses and expanded training partnerships.

For communities that depend on regional air service, the disruptions point to a larger worry about how stable their air links to smaller markets really are. Local business leaders and airport officials warn that extended service cuts could hurt tourism, business travel, and economic activity.

For now, passengers are advised to check their flight status before heading to the airport, since more schedule changes are possible in the coming days.

**Wildfire Forces Evacuations Near Redwood Canyon National Park**

**REDWOOD COUNTY, Calif.** — A wildfire near Redwood Canyon National Park sent people fleeing their homes on Tuesday, with mandatory evacuations ordered as firefighters struggled against dry weather, gusty winds and steep, rugged terrain. Officials said those conditions were feeding the fire.

The blaze, named the **Canyon Ridge Fire**, started late Monday afternoon roughly five miles east of the park's southern boundary. By Tuesday evening it had grown to an estimated **7,800 acres**, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Containment was still low. Crews were trying to protect homes, campgrounds and critical infrastructure in the mountain communities nearby.

Residents of the small towns of **Pine Creek, Alder Grove and Millstone** were ordered out, along with people in several rural neighborhoods off Highway 86. Portions of the park's gateway communities were put under an evacuation warning, and visitors there were told to be ready to leave on short notice.

"This fire is moving rapidly and conditions can change minute by minute," **Incident Commander Laura Mendes** said at an evening briefing. "Our top priority is life safety — getting people out of harm's way and giving firefighters the room they need to work."

As of Tuesday night, no deaths or serious injuries had been reported. Officials said several structures were under threat and at least two outbuildings had burned. What started the fire is still under investigation.

A stretch of **Highway 86** was shut to everyone but emergency traffic. Park officials also announced they were temporarily closing the national park's southern entrance, plus a number of backcountry trails and campgrounds. Rangers started escorting campers out of the affected areas early Tuesday. Smoke settled over nearby valleys and cut visibility across the region.

The National Weather Service put out a **red flag warning** for the area, pointing to low humidity, high temperatures and wind gusts that could top 30 mph. Fire officials said they expected those conditions to last into Wednesday, which would make containment harder.

More than **600 firefighters** have been assigned to the fire, backed by air tankers, helicopters and bulldozers. They were working through the night to cut containment lines and protect structures inside the evacuation zones.

At an evacuation center at **Redwood County High School**, displaced residents showed up with their pets, medications and a few belongings. Volunteers passed out food, water and blankets while families waited for news.

"We grabbed what we could and left," said **Pine Creek resident Maria Lopez**, who got out with her husband and two children. "You could see the glow on the ridge, and the wind was just pushing it closer."

Officials urged residents to keep an eye on emergency alerts and stay out of the area. "If you have been told to leave, leave now," Mendes said. "Do not wait to see the fire."

# Commit Message Style Guide

A good commit message says **what changed** and **why**, so someone reading the history later doesn't have to open every diff. Aim for messages that are clear, consistent, and short.

## Structure

Use this format:

```text
<type>: <short summary>

<optional body>

<optional footer>
```

### 1. Short summary
- Try to keep it to **50 characters or fewer**.
- Use the **imperative mood**: "add", "fix", "remove", not "added" or "fixes".
- Begin with a lowercase type and a colon.
- Don't put a period at the end.

Examples:
- `fix: handle null response in user service`
- `docs: clarify local setup steps`
- `refactor: simplify cache invalidation logic`

### 2. Body
Add a body when the summary alone doesn't make the change obvious.

Guidelines:
- Wrap lines at about **72 characters**.
- Say **why** you made the change before getting into how you implemented it.
- Mention context, tradeoffs, side effects, or migration notes where they matter.
- Keep paragraphs short, or use bullet points, so it's easy to read.

A handy pattern to follow:
- What problem existed?
- Why did you pick this approach?
- Are there risks or follow-up tasks?

### 3. Footer
Use footers for metadata when you need it:
- Issue references: `Refs: #123`
- Closing references: `Closes: #456`
- Breaking changes: `BREAKING CHANGE: config format has changed`

## Recommended types

Stick with a small, predictable set of types. Common ones are:
- `feat`: new functionality
- `fix`: bug fix
- `docs`: documentation only
- `refactor`: code change without behavior change
- `test`: tests added or updated
- `chore`: maintenance, tooling, dependency updates
- `perf`: performance improvement
- `build`: build system or dependency management changes
- `ci`: continuous integration changes

## Best practices

- Let each commit be **one logical change**.
- Write the message like a command:
  - "add validation for empty emails"
  - "remove deprecated API client"
- Be specific. Prefer:
  - `fix: prevent duplicate invoice creation`
  over:
  - `fix: bug fixes`
- If a commit is large or complex, explain it.
- Read the message over before you commit, since it becomes a permanent part of the project's history.

## Avoid

- Vague summaries like `update stuff` or `misc fixes`
- Overly long subjects
- Describing only the code and not the reason for it
- Mixing unrelated changes into one commit
- Leaving auto-generated messages unedited, such as `WIP` or `temp`

## Example

```text
fix: prevent retry loop on expired auth token

The client kept retrying requests after receiving a 401 response,
which caused unnecessary traffic and delayed user-facing errors.

Stop retries when the token is expired and surface a re-auth
prompt instead.

Closes: #214
```

Consistency matters more than perfection. A simple standard that everyone shares makes project history easier to read, search, and maintain.

## Installation

csvparser needs **Python 3.8 or newer** and is a regular Python package, so `pip` handles it:

```bash
pip install csvparser
```

If you're working inside a project, you'll probably want a virtual environment first:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate         # Windows
pip install csvparser
```

To check that it worked:

```bash
python -c "import csvparser; print(csvparser.__version__)"
```

Want to install from source instead? Clone the repo and do an editable install:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-org/csvparser.git
cd csvparser
pip install -e .
```

Editable mode is handy while developing, since changes you make to the local code show up right away and you don't have to reinstall.

---

## Quick Start

The library aims to make reading and validating CSV data easy. In the simplest case, you load a file and loop over the rows, each of which comes back as a dictionary.

Say you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,30,London
Bob,25,Paris
Charlie,35,Berlin
```

Here's how you'd parse it:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")
rows = parser.read()

for row in rows:
    print(row)
```

Output:

```python
{'name': 'Alice', 'age': '30', 'city': 'London'}
{'name': 'Bob', 'age': '25', 'city': 'Paris'}
{'name': 'Charlie', 'age': '35', 'city': 'Berlin'}
```

### Reading rows one at a time

With large files, iterate over the parser rather than loading everything into memory:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser

parser = CSVParser("people.csv")

for row in parser:
    print(row["name"], row["city"])
```

### Custom delimiter

If the file uses something other than a comma, pass the delimiter when you create the parser:

```python
parser = CSVParser("data.tsv", delimiter="\t")
rows = parser.read()
```

### Header validation

You can also require certain column names:

```python
parser = CSVParser(
    "people.csv",
    required_columns=["name", "age", "city"]
)

rows = parser.read()
```

If any required columns are missing, the parser raises an error right away. That way you catch malformed input before any processing starts.

---

## Error Handling

To deal with bad files gracefully, wrap the parsing in a `try`/`except` block:

```python
from csvparser import CSVParser, CSVParserError

try:
    rows = CSVParser("people.csv").read()
except CSVParserError as exc:
    print(f"Failed to parse CSV: {exc}")
```

---

## Next Steps

Once basic parsing is working, you can build on it by:

- validating row values
- converting string fields to integers, floats, or dates
- skipping empty lines
- integrating parsing into ETL scripts or web backends

For the full API, check the project documentation or the docstrings in the source code.

**The Fifth Day**

For six years, my Sunday evenings came with a low hum of dread. Nothing was actually wrong. The job was fine and my colleagues were kind. But the weekend kept disappearing on me. Saturday went to errands and recovering, and Sunday went to bracing for Monday. I was always living in the margins of my own life.

Then my company ran a pilot: four days a week, same pay, same expected output. I figured it was a trick. I assumed I'd end up working ten-hour days, or coming back to a mountain of whatever Friday had left undone.

What happened was stranger. The work shrank to fit the time. Meetings that used to wander for an hour found their point in twenty minutes. We quit scheduling gatherings to discuss other gatherings. When you only have four days, you protect them. People started saying no more often, and oddly, everything important still got done.

The research since then matches what I felt. In the 2022 UK pilot, which covered about 61 companies and roughly 2,900 workers, the large majority of firms kept the shorter week afterward. Employees reported less burnout and better sleep, and revenue held steady. Iceland's earlier trials told a similar story. None of this proves every workplace could pull it off, but it does undercut the idea that more hours automatically means more value.

That idea is the real problem. We inherited the five-day week from an industrial era, when output tracked hours on the factory floor. Most of us don't work that way anymore. Knowledge work runs on attention, and attention doesn't scale in a straight line. The fifth day was often the one where I was physically there but mentally gone, answering emails to prove I existed.

What I got back wasn't just rest, though the rest mattered. It was ordinary life. I went to the dentist without having to negotiate my calendar. I cooked a real dinner on a Friday. I spent a long afternoon with my father, who is older than he used to be, and I realized how much of our relationship had been squeezed into scraps of leftover time. A day off isn't so much a luxury as a place for the things that make a person more than an employee.

Critics worry about fairness, and they're right to. A four-day week is harder to arrange for nurses, teachers, and restaurant staff, whose work can't be shortened by cutting meetings. But that's an argument for designing it carefully, with staggered shifts, more hiring, and honest measurement. It isn't a reason to refuse to try it where it works. Some people will also cram five days into four longer ones, which misses the point. The goal isn't the same hours in fewer days. It's fewer hours, spent well.

I don't think the four-day week will fix everything. Bad managers will stay bad, and pressure will find new outlets. But I came out of that pilot with a clearer sense of what work is for. It's one part of life, not the thing life is organized around.

These days, my Sunday evenings are quiet. I notice that more than any productivity statistic.

# The Teacher Who Waited

In seventh grade, my math teacher, Mr. Okafor, did something that drove me up the wall: he wouldn't just tell me the answer.

I was stuck on a word problem about two trains. I put my hand up the way you do when you assume adults are there to clear up your confusion fast. He came over, looked at my paper, and asked, "What do you know so far?" I told him nothing. "Great," he said. "Let's write that down." And then he just waited. He wasn't impatient and he didn't sigh. He seemed like a man with the whole afternoon free. To fill the quiet, I started listing things. The trains left at different times. One of them was faster. Halfway through my own sentence, I saw how it worked.

I've been thinking about that silence for years. It showed me something that seems backwards at first: a teacher's job isn't really to hand over knowledge, but to help build a person who can go find it.

Knowing the subject does matter, of course. If you don't understand the material, you can't lead anyone through it. But I've met brilliant people who were awful teachers because they'd forgotten what not knowing feels like. Expertise can make you short with other people's confusion. Mr. Okafor treated confusion as a normal place to be, even an interesting one, and he never made me feel stupid for standing in it.

That leads to the second thing, which is that a good teacher makes it safe to be wrong. In his room, mistakes went up on the board for everyone to look at, and he examined them with curiosity instead of judgment. "Interesting," he'd say. "Where did this go sideways?" We learned to track down our own errors like detectives, not bury them like evidence. I've kept that habit as an adult, where owning up to a mistake early can be the difference between a small problem and a disaster.

The third thing is harder to put into words. Good teachers believe in you a little before you've earned it. Once Mr. Okafor handed me a problem from a competition packet meant for older kids and said, "I think you'd enjoy this one." I never solved it. But I spent a week trying, and I still remember what it felt like to be taken seriously. His expectation was like a loan, and I worked hard to pay it back.

Since then I've had teachers who were more charismatic, more entertaining, more celebrated. Some were wonderful. But when I ask myself who changed the way I think, I keep coming back to the man standing next to my desk, letting a silence run until I filled it myself.

Teaching like that takes real restraint. It would have been quicker to show me the solution, and I'd have been thankful for maybe ten minutes. What he gave me instead was slower and lasted far longer: the experience of working it out, and the quiet realization that I could.

I don't remember the answer to the train problem. I remember the waiting, and I think that's the point.

# Regional Airline Cancels Dozens of Flights as Pilot Shortage Deepens

**Skyline Air grounds routes serving smaller cities, leaving thousands of travelers scrambling**

*By Staff Reporter*

Skyline Air, a regional carrier, said Monday it will cancel about 120 flights over the next six weeks. The company blames a shortage of qualified pilots, which it says has now reached a critical point.

Eight mid-sized and rural markets will be affected, among them Cedar Falls, Marlow County, and Pine Harbor. According to a company statement, three of those communities will have no daily service at all until at least mid-March.

"We deeply regret the disruption to our customers and the communities we serve," said Dana Whitfield, Skyline's chief operating officer. "We have exhausted every option to cover these routes safely and within federal duty-time regulations. Without enough pilots, we cannot operate the schedule we promised."

Skyline says it has lost nearly 15 percent of its pilots in the past year. Many left for major carriers that offer higher salaries, signing bonuses, and faster routes to international flying. The airline now has about 340 pilots, compared with 400 last January.

Industry analysts see Skyline's situation as part of a bigger national problem. Veteran pilots are retiring in large numbers, and a federal rule requires airline captains to log 1,500 flight hours, which has thinned the pool of new hires. Regional airlines, often where future major-carrier pilots get their training, have taken the worst of it.

"Regionals are the farm system of the industry," said Marcus Tran, an aviation consultant. "When the big airlines hire aggressively, the regionals bleed talent. Then the small towns that depend on them lose air service, and it's very hard to get it back."

Passengers felt the effects right away. At Cedar Falls Regional Airport on Monday, traveler Priya Natarajan said her flight to a family wedding was canceled with just two days' notice. "I got a text and an email, and that was it," she said. "Now I'm looking at a five-hour drive to the nearest hub."

Local officials are concerned about what comes next. Cedar Falls Mayor Tom Hendricks said reliable air service matters for drawing employers and supporting local businesses. "Losing flights isn't just an inconvenience," he said. "It affects our economy."

Skyline said affected passengers can get full refunds or, where possible, be rebooked on partner airlines. The company also announced a new retention package that includes raises of up to 18 percent and a tuition-assistance program for aspiring pilots.

Whitfield said the airline hopes to have full service back by April, but she would not guarantee a timeline.

## Bike-Share FAQ

### 1. What is the bike-share service?
It's a cheap, easy, and green way to get around the city. Unlock a bike at one station, ride to where you're going, and drop it off at any available station in the network.

### 2. How do I sign up?
Use our mobile app or website. Create an account, pick a pass or membership, and add a payment method. After that, you can unlock bikes straight from the app.

### 3. What types of passes are available?
There are a few options depending on what you need: single rides, day passes, and monthly or annual memberships. Short-term passes work well for visitors, and memberships make more sense if you ride regularly. You'll find current prices on our website and in the app.

### 4. How do I unlock a bike?
Open the app and find a station nearby or an available bike. Then scan the QR code or type in the bike number, and the lock will release on its own. If something goes wrong, customer support can help.

### 5. Where can I return a bike?
Take it to any official bike-share station that has an open dock. Make sure the bike is locked firmly in place, and wait for the app to confirm the return so you don't get hit with extra charges.

### 6. Is there a time limit for rides?
Yes, and it depends on which pass or membership you bought. If you go over the ride period your pass includes, extra fees may apply. You can see your ride details in the app whenever you like.

### 7. What if a station is full?
The app will show you nearby stations that have open docks. Sometimes you may qualify for a grace period, which lets you return the bike at the next closest station.

### 8. What should I do if a bike is damaged?
If you spot a problem before or during your ride, report it in the app right away and switch to another bike if you need to. Reports help us keep the fleet safe and in good shape.

### 9. Do I need to wear a helmet?
We strongly recommend that all riders wear one, and local law may require it for certain age groups. Check your local regulations before you ride.

### 10. What happens if a bike is lost or stolen?
If a bike goes missing or is stolen while you're renting it, contact customer support right away, and file a police report if one is required. You may be charged until the bike is found or the case is resolved.

### 11. How can I contact customer support?
You can reach us through the app, the website, or by phone. Our Help section has the current contact details and service hours.

I grew up in a family where meat was ordinary the way furniture is ordinary: always there, and hardly ever noticed. We had roast chicken on Sundays, bacon on weekends, burgers in summer. Nobody at my house talked about the ethics of eating animals, because it never seemed like there was an ethical question to begin with. Meat was food, and food was what kept a family alive and brought it to the table. If we felt gratitude, it went to whoever did the cooking, not to the animal that had been killed.

What changed things for me wasn't some dramatic revelation. It was a pile-up of small discomforts. I remember standing in the grocery store looking at the packaged cuts of meat and feeling, maybe for the first time, how far away the product was from the life it had come from. The clean plastic wrap seemed built not just to keep the meat fresh but to keep me from thinking too hard. And once I started thinking, I couldn't really stop. I saw that my appetite relied on a kind of selective attention. I liked animals in the abstract, but when they were on my plate I preferred not to picture them at all.

As I understand it now, the ethical problem of eating meat starts with that avoidance. Most of us would admit animal suffering matters at least a little. We see pain in a dog, fear in a cow, agitation in a chicken. Yet our food system often treats these animals as units of production rather than living beings with experiences of their own. If it's wrong to cause suffering unnecessarily, then industrial meat production looks especially hard to defend. The scale of the confinement, mutilation, and slaughter is so vast that it's hard to grasp, and maybe that's part of why it continues. Cruelty is easier to take part in when it's hidden behind branding, routine, and convenience.

At the same time, I'm wary of turning this question into a simple moral performance. Eating meat is tangled up with culture, class, geography, and memory. For some people it's about tradition; for others it's about survival, health, or having few alternatives. I don't think ethics is helped by pretending every eater stands on equal ground, free to pick from the same options. Someone buying cheap meat to feed a family under financial strain isn't in the same position as someone who treats animal products as a luxury. Moral judgment with no social context can turn into self-congratulation.

Still, complexity shouldn't become an excuse for indifference. That nobody can live perfectly doesn't mean nobody has to try. I haven't reached a pure or final answer. I eat less meat than I used to, and when I do eat it, I feel the weight of the choice more consciously. For me, the ethics of eating meat isn't only about whether killing animals can ever be justified. It's also about whether I'm willing to let comfort silence my attention. Eating ethically, if that's even possible, may start with refusing that silence: looking steadily at what nourishes us, what it costs, and who pays the price.
