*A note: I'm an AI, so this is a fictional first-person essay rather than my own experience, written to sound the way such a reflection might.*

---

**The Smaller Person**

I was thirty-four, standing in a bakery in Lisbon, running a sentence through my head. I wanted a coffee and a custard tart. I'd practiced the whole walk over, but when the woman behind the counter looked up, every word went out of my head. I pointed and said "this." Then I said "this" again. She smiled at me kindly, the way you'd smile at a small child, and my face went hot.

That's what Portuguese taught me first: how much of who I thought I was depended on sounding competent. Back home, people came to me for answers. In that bakery I had a toddler's vocabulary and a department head's pride, and the two of them did not get along.

For months I was a shrunken version of myself. I couldn't joke or argue, and I couldn't toss out the offhand remark that makes people remember you. I'd always figured my personality was solid, but it leaned on grammar far more than I'd realized. What was left was simpler: patient, a bit earnest, confused a lot of the time. Oddly, people liked him. My neighbor, Dona Fernanda, was seventy and had never once left Portugal, and she started correcting me with real ceremony. "Not *eu sou cansado*," she'd say. "*Estou* cansado. You *are* tired, but you are not *made of* tired." I've never lost the difference between permanent and temporary states, and these days I catch myself thinking about it in English too.

The second lesson was about listening. In English I'd always listened lazily, already building my answer while the other person was still talking. In Portuguese I had to catch every word as if it had been thrown at me. So I began to notice tone, and gesture, and the pauses people left. I got better at listening in both languages, and I was a little embarrassed at how much I'd been missing.

The third lesson was that mistakes won't kill you. One night I told a whole dinner table I was "very constipated" when what I meant was embarrassed. (They're false friends, and I'll leave it there.) The table roared, somebody topped up my glass, and I felt more included than I had all week. Failing in front of people, it turns out, mostly makes them warmer toward you. I'd spent years dodging the exact thing that would have loosened me up.

Progress was invisible, until it wasn't. For a long stretch I felt stuck. Then one afternoon I realized I'd followed an entire conversation between two fast-talking taxi drivers, and I'd laughed at the right moment. Nobody handed me a certificate. It was more like a door I hadn't known was shut was simply standing open.

I still make mistakes every day, and I still hear that slight gentleness people put on for foreigners. I just don't hear it as pity anymore. I hear it as hospitality, offered to anyone willing to stand in front of strangers and be bad at something.

What I took from those years isn't really fluency. It's being willing to be the smaller person, to point and say "this" and try again. He was never lesser, that guy. He was just learning, which was the one thing I'd stopped letting myself do.

# Erie Canal

The **Erie Canal** is a historic canal in the U.S. state of New York. It links the Hudson River at Albany with Lake Erie at Buffalo. When it was finished in 1825, it became the first navigable waterway to connect the Atlantic seaboard with the Great Lakes, and it did a great deal to shape the American economy in the nineteenth century.

## History

People had been talking about a canal across upstate New York since the late 1700s. The idea only gained real momentum when Governor DeWitt Clinton took up the cause. Federal support never came through, so in 1817 he secured funding from the state instead. Critics mocked the project as "Clinton's Ditch." Work began on July 4, 1817, at Rome, New York.

Most of the digging was done by hand. Laborers, many of them Irish immigrants, worked with horses, oxen, and simple tools. The engineers, among them Benjamin Wright and James Geddes, had little formal training and learned as they went, working out ways to clear forests and stumps and to deal with swampland. The original channel ran about 363 miles (584 km) and measured 40 feet (12 m) wide and 4 feet (1.2 m) deep. It had 83 locks to handle an elevation difference of roughly 565 feet (172 m).

The canal officially opened on October 26, 1825. Clinton traveled from Buffalo to New York City in a ceremonial voyage, and along the way he symbolically poured Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean in what became known as the "Wedding of the Waters."

## Economic and social impact

The canal sharply cut both the cost and the time of moving freight. A ton of goods shipped from Buffalo to New York City had cost around $100, and afterward it cost roughly $10. Travel time fell from weeks to days. Farm products from the Midwest moved east, while manufactured goods and settlers headed west.

New York City overtook rival ports like Philadelphia and Boston to become the country's leading commercial center. Cities along the route, including Syracuse, Rochester, Utica, and Buffalo, grew quickly. The corridor also became a hub of social change, associated with religious revivalism, the women's rights movement, and abolitionism. Some historians have called western New York the "burned-over district" for this reason.

## Enlargement and modern use

The canal was enlarged between 1836 and 1862. From 1905 to 1918 it was replaced by the larger **New York State Barge Canal**, whose route incorporated rivers and lakes. In the twentieth century, railroads, then highways and the St. Lawrence Seaway, cut into commercial traffic.

These days the canal is used mainly for recreation, such as boating, cycling, and tourism along the Erie Canalway Trail. In 2000, Congress designated the Erie Canalway National Heritage Corridor to preserve its legacy. The New York State Canal Corporation still operates the canal.

## See also

- DeWitt Clinton
- Great Lakes
- Hudson River
- Transportation in New York

When I was younger, I figured the center of a city began wherever traffic got thick: the bright lights, the nonstop motion, the low growl of engines idling at red lights. A busy street felt like proof that a place mattered. If everyone was trying to get there, that must be where life was. But the older I get, the more I notice what traffic takes from a place. Conversations get cut off by sirens. A haze of fumes hangs over a summer afternoon. People squeeze along narrow sidewalks while rows of metal sit motionless in the middle of the street. So when I ask myself whether cities should ban cars from their centers, I keep landing on yes. It isn't that I dislike cars. I just think city centers should belong to people first.

It wasn't a statistic that changed my mind, though there are plenty of convincing ones about pollution and safety. It was a feeling. In the few places I've visited where cars were limited or absent, I felt a release almost right away. People walked down the middle of the street without fear. Children darted around unpredictably, the way children do, and nobody seemed annoyed with them. Outdoor tables were places to linger, not little islands in a sea of noise. The city didn't feel empty without cars. It felt newly filled with human life.

A city center is not just a corridor for getting somewhere. It's where a city shows itself to itself. Tourists form their first impressions there, office workers grab lunch, elderly people try to cross the road, protests gather, and strangers become part of a crowd. If vehicles dominate that space, we've made a strange choice about what we value. We've picked speed over encounter and convenience over community.

Of course, banning cars from city centers isn't as simple as painting over a road. The objections are real, and some are serious. Disabled people, delivery drivers, emergency services, and commuters from areas with poor public transportation can't just be wished away. Small businesses may worry about losing customers. A policy that ignores all this will feel less like progress than punishment.

That's why I don't think a ban should be absolute or careless. It should be well thought out, with exemptions, reliable public transit, better cycling infrastructure, and clear plans for deliveries and access needs. The goal isn't to wage war on drivers. It's to ask what kind of urban life we want to encourage.

Cars are useful tools, but city centers are too valuable to be built around them. If we take cars out of those spaces carefully, fairly, and with alternatives in place, we may find that what looked like a sacrifice is really a recovery. We could get cleaner air, quieter streets, and a stronger sense that the heart of a city is not its traffic but its people.

I still remember walking into my local public library as a kid and feeling like I'd stepped into a place unlike any other. It was quiet, but not stiff. It felt full, and not only of books. It felt full of possibility. I didn't have the words for what the library meant, but I knew, without being told, that I was welcome there. I didn't have to buy anything, prove anything, or be anything in particular. That feeling has stuck with me, and it's a big reason I think public libraries still matter.

These days almost any piece of information is on your phone within seconds, so it's easy to see libraries as charming but outdated. If you can order books online and search articles instantly, what's left for a library to do? To me the answer is pretty simple. A public library does a lot more than store information. It makes knowledge accessible, it gives people dignity, and it makes a community visible.

What matters most to me is that a library is one of the few truly public spaces we have left. Most places in modern life expect you to spend money if you want to stay. Cafés, stores, and entertainment venues all have an unspoken price of admission. A library asks only that you respect the shared space. You can sit, read, think, learn, or just rest. That kind of openness is rare, and it says something hopeful about what a community believes people deserve.

Libraries also matter because access to information isn't nearly as equal as we like to pretend. Not everyone has a reliable internet connection, a quiet home, up-to-date technology, or the money for books and subscriptions. For a lot of people, the library fills those gaps. It has computers, internet access, job resources, research help, language learning, and educational programs. A student can study there. A job seeker can write and submit a résumé there. An immigrant can use it as a bridge into a new community. And a lonely person can go there and feel a little less alone.

I think libraries matter, too, because they encourage a slower, more thoughtful kind of discovery. Online, algorithms mostly steer us toward what we already like. In a library, we get to wander. We pull a book off the shelf because the title surprises us, or because it happens to sit next to the one we came for. Those accidental finds can expand a life. Libraries remind us that learning isn't only about efficiency. It's also about curiosity.

And maybe most of all, public libraries still matter because they reflect a democratic ideal: knowledge shouldn't belong only to people who can afford it. A library is a quiet argument against exclusion. It says that stories, facts, history, imagination, and opportunity should be shared.

That's why libraries still feel essential to me, even now. They aren't relics of an earlier time. They're living promises. In their own humble way, they tell us a community is strongest when it invests in places where everyone is allowed to walk in and grow.

# Create Event

Creates a new event on the calendar you specify.

**Endpoint**
```
POST /v1/calendars/{calendar_id}/events
```

**Authentication:** You'll need a Bearer token with the `calendar.events.write` scope.

---

## Path Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `calendar_id` | string | The calendar's ID. Use `primary` for the user's default calendar. |

## Request Body

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `title` | string | Yes | The event title, up to 200 characters. |
| `start` | string | Yes | Start time in ISO 8601 format, e.g. `2025-07-01T14:00:00Z`. |
| `end` | string | Yes | End time, which has to come after `start`. |
| `timezone` | string | No | An IANA time zone such as `America/New_York`. If you leave it out, the calendar's time zone is used. |
| `description` | string | No | Details about the event, up to 5,000 characters. |
| `location` | string | No | A physical address or a meeting URL. |
| `attendees` | array | No | A list of objects, each with an `email` field and an optional `optional` boolean. |
| `reminders` | array | No | A list of objects, each with a `method` (`email` or `popup`) and `minutes_before`. |
| `recurrence` | string | No | An RRULE string, e.g. `FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT=10`. |
| `send_notifications` | boolean | No | Whether to email invitations. Defaults to `true`. |

## Example Request

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/calendars/primary/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "title": "Project Kickoff",
    "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
    "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
    "location": "https://meet.example.com/kickoff",
    "attendees": [
      { "email": "jordan@example.com" },
      { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true }
    ],
    "reminders": [{ "method": "popup", "minutes_before": 10 }]
  }'
```

## Success Response

**Status:** `201 Created`

```json
{
  "id": "evt_8f3k29x",
  "calendar_id": "primary",
  "title": "Project Kickoff",
  "start": "2025-07-01T14:00:00Z",
  "end": "2025-07-01T15:00:00Z",
  "status": "confirmed",
  "attendees": [
    { "email": "jordan@example.com", "response": "pending" },
    { "email": "sam@example.com", "optional": true, "response": "pending" }
  ],
  "created_at": "2025-06-20T09:12:44Z",
  "url": "https://calendar.example.com/events/evt_8f3k29x"
}
```

## Errors

| Status | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | `invalid_request` | A required field is missing, a date is malformed, or `end` is before `start`. |
| 401 | `unauthorized` | The token is missing, invalid, or expired. |
| 403 | `insufficient_scope` | The token doesn't have write permission for this calendar. |
| 404 | `calendar_not_found` | The calendar you specified doesn't exist. |
| 409 | `conflict` | An identical event already exists (only when an idempotency key is used). |
| 429 | `rate_limited` | You've sent too many requests. Wait for the time given in the `Retry-After` header, then retry. |

## Notes

- **Idempotency:** Add an `Idempotency-Key` header if you want to retry requests safely without creating duplicates.
- **Rate limit:** 60 requests per minute per user.
- **Attendee limit:** An event can have up to 200 attendees.
- **All-day events:** Pass just a date (e.g. `2025-07-01`) for both `start` and `end`. The `end` date is exclusive.

Friendship used to feel smaller to me, but closer too. When I was a kid, a friend was someone I saw at school, someone whose house I'd been to, someone whose voice I knew without having to look at a screen. If I wanted to tell them something, I had to wait until lunch, or call their home phone and hope a parent didn't pick up. That kind of friendship was slow, and sometimes frustrating, but it had a certain weight. Every interaction felt chosen. You had to make time.

Social media changed all that. At first it felt like a miracle. Friendship wasn't limited anymore by distance or schedules, or even by shyness. I could stay connected to people from old schools, summer programs, family trips, and eventually different stages of my life. Someone I hadn't seen in years could still turn up in my day through a photo, a joke, a birthday post, or a message sent after midnight. Friendship seemed continuous, as if nobody ever had to disappear completely.

There's something beautiful in that. I've gotten to see the ordinary details of my friends' lives in a way that wouldn't have been possible before: new apartments, bad haircuts, pets, travel photos, engagements, breakups, quiet victories. I've celebrated people I might otherwise have lost. Sometimes a simple reaction to a story can reopen a door. A friendship that would have faded can survive on small digital gestures. Social media has made it easier to say, "I'm still here. I still know you."

And yet it has changed friendship in ways that unsettle me. It gives the illusion of intimacy without always demanding the work intimacy takes. I can know what someone ate, where they vacationed, and what political opinion they posted, and still have no real idea how they're doing. I can feel caught up on a person's life without ever asking them a sincere question. In that way, social media can turn friendship into passive observation. We watch each other instead of actually meeting.

It has also blurred what the word "friend" means. The number can climb into the hundreds, even thousands, but that abundance can hide a different kind of loneliness. Being visible isn't the same as being known. Getting likes isn't the same as being comforted. Social media encourages performance, and friendship gets tangled up with presentation. Instead of sharing ourselves, we start curating ourselves, even for people who care about us. The pressure to seem happy, witty, successful, or unbothered can make honesty feel risky.

Still, I don't think social media has ruined friendship. I think it has exposed both its strengths and its weaknesses. It can help us stay connected, but it can't replace presence. It can start conversations, but it can't guarantee depth. The friendships that matter most in my life are the ones that survive both online and offline: the people I can send memes to but also call in a crisis, the people who notice when I go quiet, the people who know the version of me that exists beyond the profile.

Social media changed friendship by making it wider, faster, and more constant. But it also taught me that real friendship is still built the old-fashioned way, through attention, honesty, time, and care.

Tbilisi is Georgia's capital and its largest city, sitting on the banks of the Mtkvari River in the east of the country. More than a million people live there, and it serves as the country's political, economic, and cultural center. Because it lies where Europe meets Asia, the city has long been a meeting point for traders, diplomats, and artists.

The name comes from the Georgian word "tbili," which means "warm" and refers to the natural sulfur hot springs in the area. Tradition says King Vakhtang I Gorgasali of Iberia founded the city in the 5th century after he came across the springs while out hunting. Archaeologists, though, have found evidence that people were living here even earlier. Tbilisi went on to become the capital of the eastern Georgian kingdom and grew into a major urban center on the region's trade routes.

Over the centuries, many powers fought over the city, among them the Persians, Arabs, Byzantines, Seljuks, Mongols, and Ottomans. Russian imperial expansion in the 19th century left its mark too, and Tbilisi became an important administrative center of the Russian Empire in the Caucasus. After a brief period of independence and then Soviet rule, it became the capital of independent Georgia in 1991, when the Soviet Union dissolved.

The city is known for an architectural mix that reflects its layered past. The Old Town has narrow streets, traditional wooden balconies, churches, mosques, and bathhouses, while the later districts include neoclassical, Art Nouveau, Soviet modernist, and contemporary buildings. Among the best-known landmarks are Narikala Fortress, Metekhi Church, Sameba Cathedral, Rustaveli Avenue, and the historic sulfur baths of Abanotubani.

Tbilisi is also Georgia's leading center for education, the arts, and science. Tbilisi State University, one of the oldest universities in the Caucasus, is based here, along with museums, theaters, galleries, and research institutions. The Georgian National Museum, the Shota Rustaveli Theatre, and the Tbilisi Opera and Ballet Theatre are among the top cultural institutions.

The economy is diversified, resting on services, finance, tourism, transportation, and industry. Tbilisi is also the country's main transportation hub, with an international airport, railway connections, and a metro system. In recent decades it has been extensively redeveloped and modernized, though much of its historic character has survived.

Today the city is recognized for its multicultural heritage, lively public life, and distinctive urban landscape. It remains one of the most important cities in the South Caucasus and a symbol of Georgian statehood and identity.

# Library of Alexandria

The **Library of Alexandria**, in Alexandria, Egypt, was one of the largest and most prestigious libraries of the ancient world. It was founded in the early 3rd century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty and was part of a research institution called the Mouseion (Museum), which was dedicated to the Muses. Over time it came to stand for ancient learning, and in popular culture, for knowledge lost to destruction.

## History

Nobody knows exactly when it was set up, but it was probably established under Ptolemy I Soter (r. 305–282 BCE) or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 284–246 BCE). Tradition credits Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian exile, with advising on its creation, though modern scholars debate what role he actually played. The Ptolemies wanted to collect texts from all over the known world. Ancient sources say that ships coming into Alexandria's harbor were searched for books. These were copied, and sometimes the library kept the originals and gave the owners the copies instead.

## Collection and scholarship

Estimates of how much the library held vary a great deal. Ancient writers give figures anywhere from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, and these numbers are generally considered unreliable. The collection covered literature, history, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy. Most of it was in Greek, though some works were translations from other languages. Tradition holds that the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.

Prominent scholars were drawn to the library. Euclid is associated with Alexandria and wrote his *Elements* there. Eratosthenes, who served as librarian, calculated the Earth's circumference. Aristarchus of Samothrace edited Homeric texts, and Callimachus compiled the *Pinakes*, an early catalog of the collection. Herophilus and Erasistratus, meanwhile, advanced the study of anatomy in the city.

## Decline and destruction

The library didn't meet its end in a single catastrophe; it declined gradually. In 48 BCE, during his conflict in Alexandria, Julius Caesar set a fire that damaged part of the city and may have destroyed some books, though how much was lost is uncertain. Under Roman rule, funding and royal patronage fell off. Aurelian's campaign in the 270s CE devastated the district that contained the Mouseion. # Library of Alexandria

The **Library of Alexandria**, in Alexandria, Egypt, was one of the largest and most prestigious libraries of the ancient world. It was founded in the early 3rd century BCE under the Ptolemaic dynasty and was part of a research institution called the Mouseion (Museum), which was dedicated to the Muses. Over time it came to stand for ancient learning, and in popular culture, for knowledge lost to destruction.

## History

Nobody knows exactly when it was set up, but it was probably established under Ptolemy I Soter (r. 305–282 BCE) or his son Ptolemy II Philadelphus (r. 284–246 BCE). Tradition credits Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian exile, with advising on its creation, though modern scholars debate what role he actually played. The Ptolemies wanted to collect texts from all over the known world. Ancient sources say that ships coming into Alexandria's harbor were searched for books. These were copied, and sometimes the library kept the originals and gave the owners the copies instead.

## Collection and scholarship

Estimates of how much the library held vary a great deal. Ancient writers give figures anywhere from 40,000 to 700,000 scrolls, and these numbers are generally considered unreliable. The collection covered literature, history, mathematics, medicine, and philosophy. Most of it was in Greek, though some works were translations from other languages. Tradition holds that the Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek there, producing the Septuagint.

Prominent scholars were drawn to the library. Euclid is associated with Alexandria and wrote his *Elements* there. Eratosthenes, who served as librarian, calculated the Earth's circumference. Aristarchus of Samothrace edited Homeric texts, and Callimachus compiled the *Pinakes*, an early catalog of the collection. Herophilus and Erasistratus, meanwhile, advanced the study of anatomy in the city.

## Decline and destruction

The library didn't meet its end in a single catastrophe; it declined gradually. In 48 BCE, during his conflict in Alexandria, Julius Caesar set a fire that damaged part of the city and may have destroyed some books, though how much was lost is uncertain. Under Roman rule, funding and royal patronage fell off. Aurelian's campaign in the 270s CE devastated the district that contained the Mouseion. The Serapeum, a "daughter library," was destroyed in 391 CE under Bishop Theophilus. As for the story that the Arab conqueror Amr ibn al-As burned the library in 642 CE, most historians regard it as a later legend.

## Modern legacy

Egypt opened the **Bibliotheca Alexandrina** in 2002, near the ancient site. It is a modern library and cultural center meant to revive the spirit of the original institution.

- Library of Pergamum
- Septuagint

# Plugin System Documentation

## Overview

You can extend the editor with plugins instead of modifying the core application. Plugins are written in JavaScript and run in an isolated sandbox. They talk to the editor through a controlled API.

## Installing Plugins

Put your plugin folders in the user plugin directory:

- **Windows:** `%APPDATA%\Editor\plugins`
- **macOS/Linux:** `~/.config/editor/plugins`

You can also open the command palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P`) and run **Plugins: Install from Registry**. To activate new plugins, restart the editor or run **Plugins: Reload All**.

## Plugin Structure

A plugin is a folder with at least two files:

```
my-plugin/
├── manifest.json
└── index.js
```

### manifest.json

The manifest describes your plugin:

```json
{
  "name": "word-counter",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "permissions": ["editor.read", "ui.statusbar"],
  "activationEvents": ["onStartup"]
}
```

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `name` | Unique identifier, lowercase with hyphens |
| `version` | Semantic version string |
| `main` | Entry point file |
| `permissions` | APIs the plugin may access |
| `activationEvents` | When the plugin loads |

## Writing a Plugin

The entry file has to export an `activate` function. If your plugin needs to clean up after itself, export `deactivate` too.

```javascript
exports.activate = function (editor) {
  const item = editor.ui.createStatusItem();

  editor.on("textChanged", () => {
    const text = editor.document.getText();
    item.setText(`Words: ${text.split(/\s+/).length}`);
  });
};

exports.deactivate = function () {
  // Release resources here
};
```

## Core API

- **`editor.document`**: Reads and modifies the active file (`getText()`, `insert()`, `replace()`)
- **`editor.commands`**: Registers commands through `registerCommand(id, handler)`
- **`editor.ui`**: Creates status items, menus, and panels
- **`editor.on(event, callback)`**: Subscribes to events like `textChanged`, `fileSaved`, and `selectionChanged`
- **`editor.settings`**: Reads user configuration values

## Permissions

A plugin can only use the APIs it declares in its manifest. Some common permissions:

- `editor.read`: Read document contents
- `editor.write`: Modify documents
- `ui.statusbar`: Add status bar items
- `fs.read`: Read files in the workspace
- `network`: Make external requests

Users are asked to approve permissions the first time they install a plugin.

## Debugging

To see logs from `console.log` and any uncaught errors, open **Help → Toggle Plugin Console**. After you change something, run **Plugins: Reload All** to see the update right away.

## Best Practices

1. Only request the permissions you actually need.
2. Use specific activation events rather than `onStartup`, so launch stays fast.
3. Dispose of event listeners in `deactivate`.
4. Don't block. Use asynchronous calls for file and network access.

# Design Document: API Caching Layer

## Overview

I'm proposing a distributed caching layer for our web API. The goals are to take load off the database, cut response latency, and help us scale better when traffic peaks.

## Problem Statement

Right now every API request goes to the primary PostgreSQL database. When we profiled it, 80% of traffic turned out to be read-only endpoints (product catalogs, user profiles, configuration data), and a lot of those requests return identical results. At peak hours, p95 latency goes past 800ms and database CPU regularly hits 85%.

## Goals

- Get p95 latency on read endpoints under 150ms
- Cut database read load by at least 60%
- Keep data reasonably fresh, with staleness under 60 seconds for most resources
- Leave client-facing API contracts unchanged

## Non-Goals

- Caching authenticated write operations
- Replacing the database as the source of truth

## Proposed Solution

I suggest putting **Redis** between the API servers and the database as a cache-aside layer.

**Read path:** The API looks up a deterministic key in Redis (for example, `product:v1:{id}`). If it's there, it returns the cached value. If not, it queries the database, stores the result with a TTL, and returns it.

**Write path:** When a record is updated or deleted, the API invalidates the keys that relate to it. List and search results are different. Tracking what they depend on is error-prone, so they just get a short TTL (30 seconds) rather than explicit invalidation.

**Key design:**
- Keys carry a version prefix, so we can invalidate in bulk after a schema change.
- Per-user data has the user ID in the key, so one user's data can't leak to another.

**TTL strategy:**

| Resource | TTL |
|---|---|
| Configuration | 10 min |
| Product details | 5 min (plus invalidation) |
| Lists/search | 30 sec |

## Risks and Mitigations

- **Stampedes:** When a popular key expires, a lot of requests can reach the database at once. We'll use request coalescing and add random jitter (±10%) to TTLs.
- **Stale data:** We invalidate explicitly on writes and keep TTLs conservative, which limits how stale anything can get.
- **Redis outage:** The API will fall back to the database behind a circuit breaker. Performance will degrade, but requests won't fail.
- **Memory growth:** We'll set `allkeys-lru` eviction and keep an eye on memory usage.

## Rollout Plan

1. Deploy a managed Redis cluster with replication.
2. Build the caching behind a feature flag and begin with the configuration endpoints.
3. Per endpoint, roll out to 10% of traffic, then 50%, then 100%.
4. At each stage, watch hit rate, latency, and error rates.

## Success Metrics

We'll call it a success if the cache hit rate is above 75%, p95 latency is under 150ms, and database CPU stays below 50% at peak.

## Open Questions

- Should we add an in-process L1 cache for extremely hot keys?
- Would a CDN make sense for public, unauthenticated endpoints?

# Voyager 1

**Voyager 1** is a NASA space probe launched on September 5, 1977, as part of the Voyager program, which was designed to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It went up sixteen days after its twin, Voyager 2. Today it is the most distant human-made object from Earth, moving at about 17 kilometers per second (roughly 61,000 km/h) relative to the Sun.

## Mission background

The Voyager program was built around a rare alignment of the outer planets, which comes around only about once every 175 years. The alignment let spacecraft use gravity assists to travel from one planet to the next. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) built the probes, and the original funding covered just a four-year mission to Jupiter and Saturn.

## Spacecraft design

At launch, Voyager 1 had a mass of about 825 kilograms. It talks to the Deep Space Network through a 3.7-meter high-gain antenna. Three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) supply its power by turning the heat from decaying plutonium-238 into electricity. Their output drops by several watts every year, so engineers have had to turn off nonessential instruments and heaters over time. The spacecraft also carries the **Golden Record**, a gold-plated phonograph record of sounds, images, and music meant to represent life and culture on Earth.

## Planetary encounters

Voyager 1 passed closest to **Jupiter** on March 5, 1979. It revealed active volcanism on the moon Io, the first volcanic activity ever seen beyond Earth. It reached **Saturn** on November 12, 1980, and sent back detailed images of the rings and of Titan, Saturn's largest moon, whose thick atmosphere got a close look. The flyby of Titan bent the probe's path out of the ecliptic plane, which ended its tour of the planets. In 1990 it took the "Family Portrait" of the Solar System, which includes the image of Earth known as the *Pale Blue Dot*.

## Interstellar mission

On August 25, 2012, Voyager 1 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun's solar wind gives way to the interstellar medium. That made it the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. Its plasma wave instrument picked up a sharp rise in plasma density, which confirmed the crossing.

In November 2023, the probe started sending back unintelligible data because of a fault in one of its onboard computers. Engineers at JPL traced the problem to a corrupted memory chip in the flight data subsystem. In 2024 they got communication working again by relocating the affected code. That was a remarkable feat, considering the spacecraft was more than 24 billion kilometers away.

## Future

Voyager 1 is still sending back data on magnetic fields, cosmic rays, and plasma. Mission planners expect the RTGs to keep at least one instrument running into the mid-2020s, and possibly longer. With technology at roughly its 1977 level, the probe will drift silently through the Milky Way. In about 40,000 years it will pass within roughly 1.6 light-years of the star Gliese 445.

## See also

- Voyager 2
- Voyager program
- Pioneer 10
- Golden Record

# The Last Free Room

When I was nine, my family moved to a new town in the middle of winter, and for weeks I didn't know a soul. My mother was working two jobs. My father was still back in our old city, finishing out a lease. The apartment was small and quiet, and the afternoons dragged. Then one day I followed some stranger's dog down the street and wound up standing in front of the public library.

I didn't know it at the time, but it was the one place in town that wanted nothing from me.

That's what gets me now, as an adult who's learned how rare that is. Almost everywhere else, taking up space means buying something. Coffee shops expect you to order a latte. Malls want you to leave with a receipt. Even parks come with rules and closing times. The library just says: come in, sit down, stay as long as you like. I think it may be the last truly free room in American life, and I suspect we undervalue it because it asks so little of us.

People like to say libraries are obsolete, since everything's online anyway. I think that misses what a library is. Sure, it lends books, and that alone strikes me as a small miracle. One copy of a novel can pass through fifty hands. But spend an afternoon in one and you'll see it does a hundred other things. A man in a worn jacket fills out a job application on a public computer while a librarian patiently helps him attach his résumé. A teenager does her homework there because there's no internet at home. A toddler is learning to sit still through a story. Someone is getting help with tax forms, someone else is learning English, and someone is just warm for a few hours, out of the cold and safe.

None of these people are customers. They're citizens, and the library treats them that way.

The library's basic idea is also a pretty radical one: you shouldn't need money to get at knowledge. It's an old idea, but we need it more than ever. Information is everywhere these days, yet more and more of it is fenced off. Paywalls keep multiplying, and algorithms decide what we see. The library is the opposite. Its shelves are chosen by people trained to help you find what's true, not what keeps you scrolling. A librarian will answer your question without tracking you, selling your data, or nudging you toward an ad.

As for me, I spent that winter working my way through the children's section, then the adult one, then whatever a kind librarian slid across the desk with a raised eyebrow and a "Try this." I read about places I'd never get to see and lives nothing like mine. Somewhere in there I stopped feeling like the new kid. I felt like part of something bigger.

I still carry a library card, and it's one of my most prized possessions. To me it's proof of a bargain we made with each other: we'd pool our resources so that everyone, no matter their circumstances, could have access to the world.

That bargain still holds, and it's worth keeping.

**Museum Returns Looted Artifacts to Nigeria in Landmark Repatriation**

A major European museum has handed back a collection of looted artifacts to the country they came from, a move many are calling a significant step in reckoning with colonial-era plunder.

On Tuesday, at a formal ceremony, the museum gave 27 objects to Nigerian officials. They include ceremonial sculptures, carved ivory pieces, and bronze plaques taken during a 19th-century military expedition. The artifacts sat in the museum's African collections for more than a century. Once conservation work is finished, they are expected to go on display in Lagos.

Museum director Elise Hartmann called the return both "a moral responsibility and an institutional reckoning."

"These objects were acquired in circumstances that were deeply unjust," she said. "They are not simply works of art; they are part of a living cultural heritage. Returning them is the right thing to do."

The handover comes after years of pressure from Nigerian officials, scholars, and activists, who have argued that artifacts seized in colonial campaigns belong back with the communities they were taken from. The museum's own recent provenance research found that the objects were removed in a British punitive raid in 1897, then sold through European art markets before ending up in its collection.

Nigeria's Minister of Culture, Amina Bello, welcomed the return and called it "an important act of justice, dignity, and historical acknowledgment."

"For generations, these treasures were admired abroad while the people to whom they belong were denied access to them," Bello said. "Their return does not erase the past, but it helps us confront it honestly and begin to repair the damage."

The decision fits a wider shift among museums in Europe and North America, many of which are taking a harder look at how they acquired items during the colonial period. Several institutions have recently announced the return of bronzes, sacred objects, and human remains after evidence showed they were taken through violence, coercion, or theft.

The issue is still contentious, though. Some critics say museums serve a global public and should keep major collections, sharing them through loans and partnerships. Others argue that full repatriation is needed to right long-standing injustices and restore cultural sovereignty.

Experts think this return could prompt others like it. "This is not just about one museum or one set of objects," said art historian Daniel Okoye. "It signals a growing recognition that possession without consent cannot be justified indefinitely."

The museum says it will keep reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection, and it is in talks with other countries about possible returns.

For many observers, Tuesday's handover was more than a transfer of property. It was a public acknowledgment that history's wounds can no longer stay behind glass.

The museum says it will keep reviewing the provenance of hundreds of items in its collection, and it is in talks with other countries about possible returns.

For many observers, Tuesday's handover was more than a transfer of property. It was a public acknowledgment that history's wounds can no longer stay behind glass.

**The Antikythera mechanism**

The Antikythera mechanism is a hand-powered mechanical device from ancient Greece, and most people consider it the earliest known analog computer. It was built to calculate and display astronomical events: where the Sun and Moon were, the phases of the Moon, the cycles of eclipses, and possibly the movements of a few planets. It's usually dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BCE.

Divers found it in 1901 in the wreckage of a ship off the Greek island of Antikythera, which lies between Crete and the Peloponnese. What came up was a set of badly corroded bronze fragments, and at first they didn't draw much interest. Only decades later did researchers notice finely cut gears embedded in the fragments and realize how complex the thing was. Since then, modern imaging, X-ray computed tomography in particular, has uncovered much of its inner workings and inscriptions.

The mechanism sat in a wooden case about the size of a shoebox. The front had circular dials with pointers showing astronomical information, probably including the zodiac and the Egyptian calendar. Someone likely turned a hand crank to drive a train of more than 30 bronze gears, which converted that rotation into mathematical relationships matching celestial cycles. Its handling of the Moon's uneven motion was remarkably sophisticated: a pin-and-slot arrangement mimicked the changes in the Moon's speed in line with ancient Greek astronomical theory.

On the back were spiral dials for tracking longer cycles. One showed the **Metonic cycle**, a 19-year period that brings lunar months into line with the solar year. Another followed the **Saros cycle**, which was used to predict eclipses. A smaller dial seems to have marked the **Exeligmos**, a longer eclipse cycle that made predictions more accurate. The inscriptions on the device worked as a sort of operating manual, explaining what the dials and displays did.

The mechanism shows a level of technical skill that people once believed impossible in the Hellenistic world. Its precise gearing points to a sophisticated tradition of instrument-making, although no other surviving device from antiquity comes close to it in complexity. Scholars have connected it to Greek scientific traditions tied to figures like Hipparchus, Posidonius, and Archimedes, but who made it, and where, is still uncertain.

It has changed how we understand ancient science and technology, showing that Greek craftsmen and astronomers could build advanced mathematics into intricate machinery. It's often called "centuries ahead of its time," and it remains one of the most celebrated archaeological discoveries in the history of science.

**The Street That Learned to Breathe**

The first time I stood in a city center with no cars, I didn't notice anything missing. I noticed the sounds: a busker's out-of-tune accordion, a toddler shrieking with joy at a pigeon, two old men arguing over chess. It took me a full minute to work out what wasn't there, the low, constant growl I'd always mistaken for silence.

This was in a mid-sized European city, on a trip I'd mostly taken to get away from my own. At home I drive everywhere. I'm not proud of that, but I won't pretend otherwise. My downtown is something I put up with: circling for parking, paying too much for it, then walking half a mile past gray garages. So when people suggest banning cars from city centers, I get defensive right away. What about my groceries? What about my mother, who can't walk far? What about the plumber, the ambulance, the delivery driver?

Those questions deserve real answers, and the best car-free centers have them. Ambulances and fire trucks get through. Residents with disabilities get permits and drop-off zones. Deliveries happen in early-morning windows. Done well, a ban is less a wall than a filter. It says the busiest, most valuable square mile of a city shouldn't be built around the least efficient way of moving people through it.

And it is inefficient. One lane of car traffic moves maybe 2,000 people an hour. Give the same width to a tram or to pedestrians and it moves many times that. We hand over staggering amounts of prime real estate to parking empty vehicles, then wonder why rents are high and public space is scarce.

Still, I don't think the answer is a flat yes. I've seen bans imposed on cities that offered nothing in return: no reliable buses, no safe bike lanes, no affordable alternative. In those places a ban doesn't produce a lively plaza. It punishes the shift worker who commutes in from the outskirts at midnight, after the trains have stopped. Cities that ban first and build later are mostly running an experiment on their poorest residents.

So my view is conditional, but firm. Cities should move toward car-free centers, and they should earn it by building the alternatives first, or at least at the same time. Make the train faster than driving. Make the bike lane feel safe to an eleven-year-old. Then close the street, and people will barely argue.

What changed my mind wasn't statistics. It was watching that European square at dusk, when the chess players packed up and families took their place, kids weaving between café tables without a parent's hand clamped on their shoulder. Nobody was in a hurry. Nobody was in danger. I realized I had never seen a city center act like a living room before.

I still drive at home. But I've started parking at the edge of downtown and walking in. The first few times it felt like a loss. Now it feels like a small rehearsal for something better, a city where the center belongs to the people in it.

# Artemisia Gentileschi

**Artemisia Gentileschi** (8 July 1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter, and many consider her one of the most accomplished artists of her generation. She worked in the tradition of Caravaggio and became known for dramatic compositions, a naturalistic style, and strong portrayals of heroic women from myth, scripture, and history. She was also the first woman admitted to the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno in Florence.

## Early life

Artemisia was born in Rome, the eldest child of the painter Orazio Gentileschi and Prudentia Montone. Her mother died when Artemisia was around twelve. She trained in her father's workshop, where she learned drawing, how to mix color, and painting techniques. Women couldn't attend formal academies, so her education stayed largely within the studio. Her earliest signed work, *Susanna and the Elders* (1610), shows remarkable skill for someone who was only seventeen.

## Trial of Agostino Tassi

In 1611, Agostino Tassi raped Artemisia. He was a painter and a colleague of her father, hired to teach her perspective. Orazio brought charges in 1612, and a trial lasting seven months followed. Artemisia was reportedly examined under torture with thumbscrews so that her testimony could be verified. Tassi was convicted, but his sentence of exile from Rome was not enforced for long. The surviving trial transcripts are a rare record of a woman's testimony from this period.

## Career

Soon after the trial, Artemisia married the Florentine artist Pierantonio Stiattesi and moved to Florence. She did well there, winning the patronage of Cosimo II de' Medici and becoming friends with Galileo Galilei. In 1616 she joined the Accademia delle Arti del Disegno. Her work from these years includes *Judith Slaying Holofernes* (c. 1614–20) and *Self-Portrait as a Lute Player*.

Money troubles and debts pushed her back to Rome in the 1620s, and she later worked in Venice and Naples. In 1638 she joined her father at the court of Charles I in England, and after Orazio died in 1639 she finished some of his commissions. Much of her later career was spent in Naples, where she collaborated with other painters and received prominent commissions.

## Style and themes

Gentileschi's paintings are known for their strong chiaroscuro, vivid color, and emotional intensity. She often painted women such as Judith, Susanna, Esther, Bathsheba, and Cleopatra. Her heroines are physically strong and psychologically complex, unlike the more passive women her male contemporaries tended to depict.

## Legacy

For centuries after her death, Gentileschi was largely overlooked. In the 20th century, art historians, feminist scholars in particular, rediscovered her work and reassessed its significance. Her life and art have since inspired books, plays, and films, and major exhibitions, among them one at the National Gallery, London, in 2020, have cemented her reputation as a leading Baroque master.

# Migrating from Config Format v1 to v2

Version 2 of the config format has a cleaner structure, stricter typing, and more explicit names. This guide covers what changed and how to update your existing v1 files.

## Breaking Changes at a Glance

1. Top-level keys are now organized into sections.
2. Several fields have been renamed.
3. Booleans and numbers must use real YAML/JSON types, not strings.
4. Environment-specific overrides now live in a dedicated `environments` block.
5. Deprecated v1 fields are no longer supported.

## What Changed

### 1. Top-level structure

In v1, most settings sat at the root level. In v2 they're grouped into these sections:

- `server`
- `logging`
- `auth`
- `environments`

### 2. Renamed fields

Some common renames:

- `host` → `server.host`
- `port` → `server.port`
- `logLevel` → `logging.level`
- `logFile` → `logging.file`
- `enableAuth` → `auth.enabled`

### 3. Strict value types

v1 often accepted strings like `"true"` or `"8080"`. v2 wants native types instead:

- `"true"` → `true`
- `"8080"` → `8080`

### 4. Environment overrides

In v1 you'd often see flattened keys such as `dev_host` or `prod_port`. In v2 these go under:

```yaml
environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: ...
  prod:
    server:
      port: ...
```

## Example Migration

### v1

```yaml
host: "localhost"
port: "8080"
logLevel: "debug"
logFile: "/var/log/app.log"
enableAuth: "true"
dev_host: "dev.local"
prod_host: "prod.example.com"
```

### v2

```yaml
server:
  host: localhost
  port: 8080

logging:
  level: debug
  file: /var/log/app.log

auth:
  enabled: true

environments:
  dev:
    server:
      host: dev.local
  prod:
    server:
      host: prod.example.com
```

## Removed Fields

These v1 fields don't exist in v2:

- `timeoutMs` — replaced by `server.timeout`, which is in seconds
- `authModeLegacy` — removed; use `auth.provider` instead
- `debug` — replaced by `logging.level: debug`

## Tips

- Validate your file against the v2 schema before you deploy.
- Update any automation scripts that read the old field names.
- Look out for quoted booleans and numbers, since they now fail validation.
- Try the migration in a staging environment first, and do it incrementally.

## Checklist

- [ ] Nest root settings under the right sections
- [ ] Rename deprecated keys
- [ ] Convert stringified booleans and numbers to native types
- [ ] Move environment-specific values into `environments`
- [ ] Remove unsupported legacy fields

When you've done all of that, your configuration should be fully compatible with version 2.

# photodate

Rename your photos after the date they were taken. `photodate` reads the EXIF metadata and gives each file a consistent, sortable name like `2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg`.

## Features

- Pulls the original capture date from EXIF data
- Uses the file's modified time if there's no EXIF
- Filename templates you can customize
- Dry-run mode, so you can preview changes first
- Handles duplicate timestamps automatically
- Undo for the most recent run
- Works with JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, and common RAW formats

## Installation

With pip:

```bash
pip install photodate
```

Or from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/photodate.git
cd photodate
pip install .
```

You'll need Python 3.9 or newer.

## Usage

```bash
photodate [OPTIONS] PATH...
```

`PATH` can be one or more files or directories.

### Quick start

See what would change before touching anything:

```bash
photodate --dry-run ~/Pictures/vacation
```

Then rename for real:

```bash
photodate ~/Pictures/vacation
```

To include subfolders:

```bash
photodate --recursive ~/Pictures
```

## Options

| Option | Description |
|---|---|
| `-n`, `--dry-run` | Show the planned renames without changing anything |
| `-r`, `--recursive` | Process directories recursively |
| `-f`, `--format TEMPLATE` | Filename template (default: `%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S`) |
| `--fallback [mtime\|skip]` | What to do when EXIF is missing (default: `mtime`) |
| `--prefix TEXT` | Add a prefix to every filename |
| `--lowercase-ext` | Convert file extensions to lowercase |
| `--undo` | Revert the last run |
| `-v`, `--verbose` | Print every rename |

## Templates

Templates use standard `strftime` codes:

```bash
photodate --format "%Y/%m/IMG_%Y%m%d_%H%M%S" photos/
```

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `%Y` | Four-digit year |
| `%m` | Month (01–12) |
| `%d` | Day of month |
| `%H` `%M` `%S` | Hour, minute, second |

## Duplicate timestamps

Burst shots often end up with the same timestamp. If names collide, `photodate` adds a counter to the end:

```
2024-07-14_15-32-08.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_2.jpg
2024-07-14_15-32-08_3.jpg
```

It never overwrites existing files.

## Undo

Every run writes a log to `~/.photodate/last_run.json`. To revert a run:

```bash
photodate --undo
```

Only the most recent run can be undone.

## Contributing

Bug reports and pull requests are welcome. Please run `pytest` before you submit changes.

## License

MIT

# Museum Returns 27 Looted Artifacts to Nigeria in Landmark Ceremony

**Benin bronzes and ceremonial objects will go on display in Benin City after more than a century abroad**

*Hartwell, England* — A regional museum in northern England formally handed 27 artifacts back to Nigeria on Tuesday. The objects were taken in 1897 during a colonial-era military expedition, and the handover brought a decade of negotiations to a close.

At a ceremony attended by diplomats, museum staff and members of the Edo diaspora community, the Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments. The items include brass plaques, carved ivory pieces and a ceremonial staff that once belonged to the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

"These are not simply objects," said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, who led the Nigerian delegation. "They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes."

British forces attacked Benin City in 1897 and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many were later sold at auction or passed to private collectors and institutions across Europe and North America. The Hartwell museum got its pieces in 1934, through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision came after extensive provenance research that confirmed where the objects came from beyond reasonable doubt. "We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," she said. "The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

The return comes as Western institutions face growing pressure to deal with colonial-era acquisitions. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States and Scotland have returned parts of their Benin collections, while the British Museum still faces calls to restitute its much larger holdings.

Not everyone welcomes the trend. Some curators argue that universal museums let global audiences encounter a range of cultures. Others have worried about conservation capacity, though supporters of restitution point out that Nigeria is building the Edo Museum of West African Art, a major facility designed by architect David Adjaye, to house returned works.

# Museum Returns 27 Looted Artifacts to Nigeria in Landmark Ceremony

**Benin bronzes and ceremonial objects will go on display in Benin City after more than a century abroad**

*Hartwell, England* — A regional museum in northern England formally handed 27 artifacts back to Nigeria on Tuesday. The objects were taken in 1897 during a colonial-era military expedition, and the handover brought a decade of negotiations to a close.

At a ceremony attended by diplomats, museum staff and members of the Edo diaspora community, the Hartwell Museum of World Cultures transferred legal ownership of the collection to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments. The items include brass plaques, carved ivory pieces and a ceremonial staff that once belonged to the royal court of the Kingdom of Benin.

"These are not simply objects," said Dr. Amara Okonkwo, who led the Nigerian delegation. "They are records of our history, our artistry, and our identity. For generations, our communities have studied these works through photographs in foreign books. Today, that changes."

British forces attacked Benin City in 1897 and removed thousands of items from the royal palace. Many were later sold at auction or passed to private collectors and institutions across Europe and North America. The Hartwell museum got its pieces in 1934, through a bequest from the family of a former naval officer.

Museum director Helen Marsh said the decision came after extensive provenance research that confirmed where the objects came from beyond reasonable doubt. "We had to ask ourselves what responsibility we have when we know how an object came to us," she said. "The answer, ultimately, was clear. Holding onto them was no longer defensible."

The return comes as Western institutions face growing pressure to deal with colonial-era acquisitions. In recent years, museums in Germany, the United States and Scotland have returned parts of their Benin collections, while the British Museum still faces calls to restitute its much larger holdings.

Not everyone welcomes the trend. Some curators argue that universal museums let global audiences encounter a range of cultures. Others have worried about conservation capacity, though supporters of restitution point out that Nigeria is building the Edo Museum of West African Art, a major facility designed by architect David Adjaye, to house returned works.

For Chidi Eze, a London-based university student of Edo descent who came to the ceremony, the moment was deeply personal. "My grandmother used to tell me stories about the palace and the bronzes," he said. "I never thought I would see any of this come home in my lifetime."

The artifacts will be flown to Lagos next week and then taken on to Benin City, where they are expected to go on public display by early next year.

Boredom gets a bad rap. We talk about it like a minor curse, something to dodge as urgently as hunger or loneliness. A boring class, a boring conversation, a boring afternoon: they all feel like design flaws, proof that life isn't entertaining us the way it should. I used to agree. If I was stuck in line, sitting on a bus, or staring at the ceiling with nothing to do, I'd grab my phone almost without thinking. Every empty space in my day was a problem to be solved. It took me a while to see that boredom wasn't always emptiness. Sometimes it was an opening.

I first met boredom in its purest form on summer afternoons as a kid. The heat was too heavy to run around outside, the TV had nothing good on, and my friends were away. At first those afternoons felt unbearable. I remember pacing from room to room, telling anyone who'd listen that there was "nothing to do." But once the complaining had worn itself out, something odd usually happened. I'd start building strange worlds out of ordinary things. Blankets turned into forts, notebooks into newspapers for imaginary cities, and a box of mismatched buttons into treasure. Boredom was the threshold I had to cross before my imagination could get to work.

That pattern didn't go away as I got older. It just got harder to spot. Adult life is full of ways to escape boredom, many of them glowing in the palm of your hand. The second a task gets repetitive or a silence starts to stretch, a distraction is right there. But I've found that constant stimulation leaves me feeling strangely thin, as if my attention has been broken into so many pieces that none of them can settle anywhere. Boredom does the opposite and gathers me back together. It slows time down enough for the thoughts I've been avoiding, or been too busy to hear, to float up.

Some of my clearest ideas have shown up in boring moments: folding laundry, walking a route I know by heart, sitting through the first uneventful minutes of a delayed train. In those spaces my mind wanders, and wandering isn't the same as wasting time. Often it's where reflection begins. Boredom strips away urgency and invites a different kind of attention, one that's less efficient but roomier. It lets memory, curiosity, and even discomfort speak. Without it, I suspect I'd know less about what I really think.

Boredom has a moral value too. Being bored means facing the fact that not every moment exists for our amusement. The world doesn't owe us constant novelty. Learning to put up with tedium, whether that means sitting still in a waiting room, listening through a quiet pause, or letting an afternoon unfold without demanding instant gratification, can be a form of patience. It teaches humility. It reminds us that a meaningful life isn't made only of thrilling scenes but also of ordinary stretches that ask for endurance, presence, and invention.

I still dislike boredom sometimes. I still reach for distraction more often than I intend to. But I no longer see boredom as a void to fill as fast as possible. I see it as a necessary interval, a pause where something subtler can emerge. In a culture that fears silence and worships stimulation, boredom may be one of the last places where the mind can hear itself think.

# Contributing Guide

Thanks for wanting to help out with our open-source documentation website! We welcome all kinds of contributions, whether that's fixing a typo, making something clearer, adding new content, or suggesting changes to how things are structured.

## Ways to Contribute

Here are some things you can do:

- Fix spelling, grammar, or formatting issues
- Clarify existing explanations
- Add examples, tutorials, or reference material
- Report outdated or incorrect information
- Improve accessibility and readability
- Suggest better navigation or organization

Not sure your idea fits? Go ahead and open an issue first.

## Before You Start

Take a few minutes to:

- Read through the existing documentation to get a feel for its style and structure
- Search open issues and pull requests so you don't duplicate someone else's work
- Check whether anyone has already started a discussion about the change you have in mind

If you're planning a larger change, we'd suggest opening an issue before you write any content. It helps everyone get on the same page and saves time.

## Getting Started

1. Fork the repository
2. Create a new branch for your changes
3. Make your edits
4. Preview the site locally if you can
5. Commit your changes with a clear message
6. Open a pull request

Give your branch a descriptive name, like `fix-installation-typo` or `add-api-auth-guide`.

## Writing Guidelines

To keep the docs consistent:

- Write in clear, direct language
- Keep paragraphs short and headings descriptive
- Favor examples over abstract explanations
- Use the same terminology across pages
- Link to related pages where it helps
- Avoid jargon you don't need

If you're adding technical content, make sure your examples are accurate and easy to follow. If you include a command or code snippet, test it when you can.

## Style and Formatting

Please follow the project's formatting conventions, including:

- Markdown structure and heading levels
- Code blocks with language tags
- File naming patterns
- Internal linking style

If the repository has linting or formatting tools, run them before you submit your pull request.

## Pull Request Expectations

A good pull request:

- Clearly explains what changed
- Explains why the change is needed
- Stays focused on a single topic when possible
- Includes screenshots or previews for visual changes, if relevant

Please be open to feedback. Reviews are a normal part of the process, and working together makes the end result better.

## Reporting Issues

If you spot a problem but don't want to submit a fix yourself, open an issue. Please include:

- A clear title
- A link to the affected page
- A description of the problem
- A suggestion, if you have one

## Code of Conduct

Please be respectful and constructive in all your interactions. We want this project to be welcoming to contributors of every experience level.

## Thank You

Every contribution, big or small, helps make the documentation better for everyone. We really appreciate your time, effort, and ideas.

When people mourn the decline of letter writing, they usually start with nostalgia: the romance of envelopes, the elegance of stamps, the small thrill of recognizing a familiar handwriting before you've read a word. That's all real. But losing letters costs us more than a charming old ritual. It costs us a way of thinking, a way of feeling, and a way of being present to each other.

A letter asks something different of us than a text or an email does. It asks us to sit still long enough to figure out what we actually want to say. Most modern communication is built around speed. We reply fast, edit where no one can see, send half-formed thoughts, and jump in to fill any silence before it has a chance to deepen. A letter moves at the pace of reflection. Writing it, sealing it, mailing it, and waiting for it to arrive all take time, and that time encourages an honesty that is more deliberate and less impulsive. You don't usually spend a letter on what you had for lunch or on some passing irritation. You collect yourself and turn experience into language, and in the process you often understand your own mind a little better.

I think this is one of the quietest losses. Without letters, we lose a private workshop for the self. A letter isn't quite a conversation and isn't quite a diary. It sits in the intimate space between them. It's personal, but it's aimed outward: you aren't confiding in the void, you're reaching toward one particular person. That matters. In letters we tend to become slightly better versions of ourselves, more thoughtful, more generous, more willing to explain what we mean. Writing to someone we love can refine our character as well as our words.

Letters also hold on to feeling in a way instant messages rarely manage. A text can say "I miss you," but a letter carries the physical evidence that someone made it with their hands. The pressure of the pen, the slant of the lines, the crossed-out words, the note squeezed into the margin as an afterthought: none of that is mere decoration. These are traces of a living moment. A letter is language, but it's also an object. It travels through weather and across distance. You can tuck it in a drawer, open it again years later, and find that it brings back a version of a person you'd lost. Holding an old letter, you meet not only what someone felt but how they moved through time.

Giving up letters also wears down our patience with absence. Letters teach us to wait, and the waiting isn't empty. It deepens affection and gives longing room to ripen into attention. These days we can reach anyone instantly, so we tend to expect access rather than presence, and we mistake constant contact for closeness. But closeness doesn't always come from frequency. Sometimes it comes from concentration, from choosing words carefully, from speaking across a silence instead of erasing it.

I don't think we have to reject newer ways of communicating in order to grieve what letters gave us. Texts are useful, email is efficient, and phone calls are immediate. But letters gave us something those forms seldom do: a lasting record of thought shaped by time and care. When we stop writing them, we lose an art, yes, but also a human tempo. We lose one of the few kinds of communication that asks us to slow down enough to mean what we say.

# Migrating Configuration Files from v1 to v2

This guide walks through what changed between v1 and v2 of the configuration format and how to update your files. All examples are in YAML.

## Summary of Changes

| Area | v1 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Version field | Optional | **Required** (`version: 2`) |
| Server settings | Flat keys | Nested under `server` |
| Timeouts | Integers (seconds) | Duration strings (`"30s"`) |
| Environment variables | `$VAR` | `${VAR}` or `${VAR:-default}` |
| Booleans | `yes`/`no` accepted | `true`/`false` only |
| `log_file` | Supported | Removed; use `logging.output` |

## Step 1: Add the Version Field

Put this at the top of every file. A v2 parser will reject any file that doesn't have it.

```yaml
version: 2
```

## Step 2: Nest Server Settings

The flat `host`, `port`, and `timeout` keys now go under `server`.

**v1**
```yaml
host: 0.0.0.0
port: 8080
timeout: 30
```

**v2**
```yaml
server:
  host: 0.0.0.0
  port: 8080
  timeout: "30s"
```

## Step 3: Convert Timeouts to Durations

Every time value has to be a string with a unit: `ms`, `s`, `m`, or `h`. A bare integer now causes a validation error. In v1 the unit was implicitly seconds, and that caused confusion.

## Step 4: Update Environment Variable Syntax

Change `$DB_PASSWORD` to `${DB_PASSWORD}`. You can also give a variable a fallback value now:

```yaml
database:
  password: ${DB_PASSWORD:-changeme}
```

If you need a literal dollar sign, escape it as `$$`.

## Step 5: Replace Deprecated Options

`log_file` is gone. Use the `logging` block instead:

**v1**
```yaml
log_file: /var/log/app.log
```

**v2**
```yaml
logging:
  output: /var/log/app.log
  level: info
```

## Step 6: Fix Boolean Values

Swap `yes`, `no`, `on`, and `off` for `true` or `false`. v2 follows YAML 1.2, which doesn't treat the older forms as booleans anymore.

## Automated Migration

There's a converter that handles most of this for you:

```bash
config-tool migrate --from 1 --to 2 config.yaml -o config.v2.yaml
```

Look over the output before you deploy it. The tool can't work out the right `logging.level` on its own, so it defaults to `info`.

## Validating the Result

```bash
config-tool validate config.v2.yaml
```

If it reports errors, fix them. The messages include line numbers.

## Rollback

Hang on to your v1 files until v2 has run successfully in production. v1-compatible releases can still read v1 files, but v2 files aren't backward compatible.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Unquoted durations:** `30s` works, but `30` fails.
- **Unescaped `$`:** A password containing `$` may get misread as a variable.
- **Mixed versions:** Any included files must all use the same version.

# Atacama Desert

The **Atacama Desert** (Spanish: *Desierto de Atacama*) is a plateau of desert on the Pacific coast of western South America. It stretches along a strip of land about 1,600 km (1,000 mi) long, most of it in northern Chile. Many consider it the driest desert in the world outside the polar regions, and it's also one of the oldest continuously arid places on the planet.

## Geography

The desert sits between the Pacific Ocean and the Andes Mountains, running from Peru's southern border down to around La Serena in Chile. It covers roughly 105,000 km² (41,000 sq mi), although broader definitions that take in neighboring arid regions put the figure higher. You'll find salt flats (*salares*), sand dunes, rocky plains, and volcanic peaks here. In the east of the region lies the Salar de Atacama, Chile's largest salt flat.

## Climate

Several factors combine to make the place so dry. The Andes keep moisture from the Amazon Basin out from the east, while on the Pacific side the cold Humboldt Current and a persistent subtropical high-pressure system hold rainfall back. Some weather stations in the interior have never recorded any rain at all, and in many areas average annual precipitation is under 15 mm (0.6 in). There's evidence that parts of the desert have been hyperarid for millions of years.

Even so, the coast gets a lingering fog called *camanchaca*, which supplies moisture to some plants and animals.

## Ecology

Plant life is thin, but specialized organisms do manage to live here, among them cacti, lichens, and hardy shrubs. Now and then, in years of unusually heavy rain that are often tied to El Niño, parts of the desert burst into bloom in what's known as the *desierto florido* ("flowering desert"). Animals include vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and many reptiles and insects. Researchers have also looked at microbial life in the soils, which are sometimes likened to those of Mars.

## History and economy

For thousands of years the region was home to Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures. In the 19th century the desert gained economic importance because of its nitrate (saltpeter) and guano deposits, both vital to making fertilizer. The struggle for control of these resources helped bring about the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), in which Chile took territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Mining dominates the economy today, especially copper and lithium. Chuquicamata is one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

High altitude, dry air, and very little light pollution make the desert one of the best places on Earth to observe the sky. Its facilities include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, which houses the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Popular destinations include San Pedro de Atacama, the Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and a number of high-altitude lagoons.

Now and then, in years of unusually heavy rain that are often tied to El Niño, parts of the desert burst into bloom in what's known as the *desierto florido* ("flowering desert"). Animals include vicuñas, guanacos, foxes, flamingos in the salt lakes, and many reptiles and insects. Researchers have also looked at microbial life in the soils, which are sometimes likened to those of Mars.

## History and economy

For thousands of years the region was home to Indigenous peoples, including the Atacameño (Lickanantay) and Chinchorro cultures. In the 19th century the desert gained economic importance because of its nitrate (saltpeter) and guano deposits, both vital to making fertilizer. The struggle for control of these resources helped bring about the War of the Pacific (1879–1884), in which Chile took territory from Bolivia and Peru.

Mining dominates the economy today, especially copper and lithium. Chuquicamata is one of the largest open-pit copper mines in the world.

## Astronomy and science

High altitude, dry air, and very little light pollution make the desert one of the best places on Earth to observe the sky. Its facilities include the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the Paranal Observatory, which houses the Very Large Telescope.

## Tourism

Popular destinations include San Pedro de Atacama, the Valle de la Luna, the El Tatio geysers, and a number of high-altitude lagoons.

# The Slow Arithmetic of Walking

I never planned on becoming a person who walks. My car went into the shop for a week, and the bus to my office meant a transfer that tacked on forty minutes. So one gray Tuesday I just left the house on foot, grumbling, figuring I'd work something out along the way.

What I worked out, somewhere around the third mile, was that I hadn't been alone with my thoughts in years.

Walking is a funny kind of attention. It's too slow to be about getting somewhere and too fast to be about standing still. Your body has a job, but your mind gets off the leash. Problems I'd been clenching my jaw over for weeks loosened up on their own. I'd turn a corner and suddenly know how to word the difficult email, or realize I'd been angry at my brother for the wrong reason. Nietzsche claimed that all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking. I can't speak for the great ones, but the useful ones do seem to show up that way.

When the car came back, I kept walking. Mornings, mostly, before the day started making its demands. I got to know my neighborhood the way you know a person, not the way you know a map. There was the man who watered his tomatoes in a faded bathrobe and raised one finger in greeting, like a conductor cueing a single violin. There was the corner where the smell of baking bread drifted out of a vent at exactly 6:40. There was a persimmon tree I'd passed a hundred times before I noticed it was heavy with fruit, bright as lanterns against the bare branches. How much else, I wondered, had I driven right past?

The habit has its own quiet discipline. Some days it rains and I go anyway, and those turn out to be the best ones: the streets rinsed and empty, my footsteps keeping time. Some days I'm tired or sad and the walk doesn't fix anything, but it lets me carry the sadness at a more manageable pace. Sorrow, I've found, is easier to bear at three miles an hour.

I've come to love the arithmetic of it, too. A mile is about two thousand steps, and a good walk is a few thousand more. No single step feels like an accomplishment, and that's the point. Nobody applauds one step. But they pile up like pennies in a jar into something substantial: a year of mornings, a body stronger than it used to be, a mind a little less cluttered.

I think a lot now about how much of modern life is built to spare us effort, and in sparing us effort, spares us experience too. Walking won't take that deal. It asks for your time and gives back something you didn't know you were missing: the texture of a place, the rhythm of your own breath, the odd peace of being exactly as fast as you are.

Tomorrow morning I'll lace up my shoes again. I don't know what I'll think about. That's the whole idea.
