# Battle of Hastings

The **Battle of Hastings** took place on 14 October 1066. On one side was the Norman-French army of William, Duke of Normandy; on the other, an English army led by the Anglo-Saxon king, Harold Godwinson. The fighting happened about 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, near the modern town of Battle in East Sussex. The Normans won decisively, and their victory kicked off the Norman Conquest of England.

## Background

King Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, which left the succession up in the air. Harold Godwinson, the powerful Earl of Wessex, was crowned king almost at once. William of Normandy wasn't having it. He said Edward had promised him the throne, and that Harold had sworn an oath to back his claim. There was a third contender too: the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada, who pressed his own claim and invaded northern England in September 1066.

Harold went north and beat Hardrada at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Just a few days later, on 28 September, William's invasion fleet landed at Pevensey on the Sussex coast. Harold rushed his army back south, covering about 250 miles in roughly two weeks.

## Battle

Harold's men took up a defensive position on Senlac Hill and formed a shield wall along the ridge. His army was mostly infantry, a mix of elite housecarls and the fyrd, who were less well equipped. William had infantry, archers and crossbowmen, plus a sizeable cavalry force.

The fighting started in the morning. Norman archers shot uphill, but it did little good. Infantry and cavalry attacks came next, and they too failed to break the shield wall. At one point a rumour went around that William was dead, and he is said to have lifted his helmet to prove he was alive. Some Norman troops fell back, and some English soldiers chased them down the hill, only to be cut down when the Normans turned around. Historians still debate whether the Normans used feigned retreats on purpose.

As the day went on, the English line grew weaker. Harold was killed late in the day. The traditional story is that an arrow hit him in the eye, as shown in the Bayeux Tapestry, though that is disputed. Once their king had fallen, the English forces broke and ran.

## Aftermath

William kept consolidating his position, accepting submission from English leaders, and was crowned King of England at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066. Later he founded Battle Abbey on the site of the battle. The conquest changed English society, language, law and landholding profoundly.

## See also

- Norman Conquest
- Bayeux Tapestry
- Battle of Stamford Bridge

**Transit Workers Strike, Leaving Commuters Scrambling Across the City**

Thousands of commuters dealt with long delays and disruptions Tuesday after public-transit workers walked off the job. The strike shut down most bus, subway, and tram service across the city.

It started shortly after midnight, after weeks of failed contract talks between the Transit Workers Union and the Metropolitan Transit Authority. The union says its members want higher wages, stronger job protections, and better staffing. Leaders argue that workers have spent years under growing pressure from rising living costs and ongoing labor shortages.

"This strike is a last resort," union president Maria Delgado told a crowd at an early morning rally outside the transit authority's headquarters. "Our members keep this city moving every day, but they're being asked to do more with less. We need a contract that reflects the value of their work and guarantees safe, reliable service for the public."

Transit officials said they were disappointed by the walkout and warned of severe economic consequences if it drags on for several days. The authority said in a statement that it had offered a "fair and responsible" contract package with pay increases and benefit protections. It claimed, though, that the union's demands would put an unsustainable burden on a transit budget that is already strained.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement as quickly as possible," said Daniel Mercer, the authority's chief executive. "We urge union leadership to return to the bargaining table so we can restore service for the millions who depend on public transportation."

By dawn, commuters were crowding rideshare pick-up zones, squeezing onto the limited regional rail service, and lining up at bike-share stations. Downtown streets were jammed as more people took cars, taxis, and carpools to work. Several schools reported higher-than-usual absences, and some businesses said staff were arriving late or working remotely when they could.

City officials urged residents to avoid nonessential travel. They announced temporary steps to ease congestion: expanded bike lanes, extra traffic officers at major intersections, and more commuter-rail capacity. The mayor's office said it was watching the situation closely and encouraging both sides to resume talks with the help of a state-appointed mediator.

For many riders, the strike was a reminder of how much everyday life depends on public transit. "I understand why workers are upset, but this is chaos," said commuter Jasmine Lee, who spent nearly two hours getting to her office. "So many people rely on these trains and buses. I just hope they settle this soon."

Negotiations were expected to continue Tuesday afternoon, though neither side said how close it was to a deal. Until one is reached, residents are bracing for more disruption and an unpredictable commute.

**Artemisia Gentileschi** (1593 – c. 1656) was an Italian Baroque painter, and today she's counted among the most important artists of the seventeenth century. She was one of the first women to make a professional success of painting, a field dominated by men at the time, and she's best known for her powerful portrayals of biblical and mythological heroines.

Artemisia was born in Rome, the daughter of the painter **Orazio Gentileschi**, who gave her her first artistic training. She was strongly influenced by **Caravaggio**, whose dramatic light and shadow, emotional intensity, and naturalism shaped her style. Women were restricted in their artistic education back then, but she showed remarkable skill from a young age. One of her earliest known works, **_Susanna and the Elders_** (1610), already conveys psychological tension and female experience with unusual force.

A defining event in her life was the 1612 trial of **Agostino Tassi**, a painter who had raped her. The trial put Artemisia under public scrutiny and had her tortured to verify her testimony, and it has become central to how people interpret her life and art today. Soon afterward she married the Florentine painter **Pierantonio Stiattesi** and moved to Florence, where her career took off. In 1616 she became the first woman admitted to the **Accademia delle Arti del Disegno**, a significant mark of her professional standing.

She produced many of her most famous paintings during her years in Florence, and later in Rome, Venice, and Naples. Among them are **_Judith Slaying Holofernes_**, **_Judith and Her Maidservant_**, **_Lucretia_**, and **_Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting_**. Her works often show women from history, scripture, and legend at moments of crisis, courage, or revenge. Such subjects weren't unique in Baroque art, but Artemisia's handling of them has been widely praised for its intensity, dignity, and emotional complexity.

She also worked for elite patrons across Italy and beyond. Naples, where she spent time, became an important center of her later career. She probably traveled to London in the late 1630s to join her father at the court of **Charles I of England**, where she may have contributed to court commissions before going back to Naples.

After her death, Artemisia Gentileschi was overshadowed for many years by her male contemporaries, and she was often remembered mainly through her biography. Since the twentieth century, though, her reputation has risen considerably. Scholars have stressed both her technical achievement and her originality within Baroque painting. Now she's celebrated not just as a pioneering woman artist but as a major painter whose work stands alongside that of the leading masters of her age.

# VoltHaus Recalls 42,000 Home Batteries Over Overheating Risk

**Austin startup reports 31 overheating incidents, including 6 small fires, but no injuries**

AUSTIN, Texas — VoltHaus, the fast-growing home energy startup, said Tuesday it is voluntarily recalling about 42,000 HearthCell 10 residential batteries. The company found a defect that can make the units overheat and, in rare cases, catch fire.

The recall applies to units made between March 2022 and August 2023 and sold in the U.S. and Canada. VoltHaus says it has received 31 reports of overheating worldwide. In six of those, the unit smoldered or caught fire. Nobody was hurt, though two homeowners reported minor damage to garage walls.

The company traced the problem to a batch of internal wiring connectors from a third-party manufacturer. In certain conditions, like repeated rapid charging in high ambient temperatures, the connectors can wear down and build up resistance, which produces extra heat.

"Safety is the foundation of everything we build, and we fell short here," Dana Okafor, VoltHaus co-founder and CEO, said in a statement. "We are contacting every affected customer directly, and we will repair or replace every unit at no cost."

The HearthCell 10 sells for about $8,900 installed and stores solar energy for use at night or during outages. VoltHaus has sold roughly 60,000 units since it launched in 2021, so the recall touches a big share of the batteries out in the field.

To see if a unit is affected, customers can enter its serial number, which is on a label on the right side of the unit, at the company's recall website. VoltHaus tells owners of affected units to put the battery in "limited mode" through its mobile app. That caps charging speed and cuts down on heat until a technician can do the repair. Owners who can't get into the app should call the company's dedicated hotline.

Technicians will swap out the connectors, which takes about two hours. Repairs should start next week, and homes with batteries installed in attached garages or living spaces will go first.

Analysts say the recall could strain the young company's finances. VoltHaus raised $120 million in a funding round last year and has been getting ready for a public offering. "A recall of this size is expensive, but the bigger risk is reputational," said Marcus Lindqvist, an energy storage analyst at Brightline Research. "How they handle the next few weeks will matter more than the defect itself."

A spokesperson said the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission is reviewing the recall.

# csvkit-lite

csvkit-lite is a small Python library for parsing CSV files. It has no dependencies, and it handles type inference, headers, and streaming.

## Requirements

- Python 3.8 or newer
- No third-party dependencies

## Installation

You can install it from PyPI with pip:

```bash
pip install csvkit-lite
```

If you'd rather have the latest development version, install straight from GitHub:

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/example/csvkit-lite.git
```

If you want to keep things isolated, use a virtual environment:

```bash
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate    # On Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install csvkit-lite
```

To check that it worked:

```bash
python -c "import csvkit_lite; print(csvkit_lite.__version__)"
```

## Quick Start

Say you have a file called `people.csv`:

```csv
name,age,city
Alice,34,Boston
Bob,28,Denver
Carol,41,Austin
```

### Reading rows as dictionaries

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv

for row in read_csv("people.csv"):
    print(row["name"], row["age"])
```

The first line is treated as a header by default, and each row comes back as a dictionary.

### Automatic type conversion

Turn on type inference and numbers and booleans get converted for you:

```python
rows = list(read_csv("people.csv", infer_types=True))
print(rows[0]["age"] + 1)   # 35, since age is an int
```

### Custom delimiters and headers

For tab-separated or semicolon-separated files, use the `delimiter` option. If the file has no header row, give it your own column names:

```python
rows = read_csv(
    "data.tsv",
    delimiter="\t",
    header=False,
    columns=["id", "score", "label"],
)
```

### Streaming large files

`read_csv` returns a generator, so rows are read lazily. That keeps memory usage low even with large files:

```python
total = 0
for row in read_csv("huge.csv", infer_types=True):
    total += row["amount"]
print(total)
```

### Loading everything at once

If you just want a plain list, wrap the call in `list()`:

```python
data = list(read_csv("people.csv"))
```

## Handling Errors

A malformed row raises a `CSVParseError`, which includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

try:
    rows = list(read_csv("broken.csv"))
except CSVParseError as err:
    print(f"Problem on line {err.line}: {err}")
```

If you'd rather ignore bad rows, pass `skip_errors=True`.

## Next Steps

- Run the tests with `pytest`
- Read the full API reference in the `docs/` folder
- Report bugs on the GitHub issue tracker

A malformed row raises a `CSVParseError`, which includes the line number:

```python
from csvkit_lite import read_csv, CSVParseError

except CSVParseError as err:

```

If you'd rather ignore bad rows, pass `skip_errors=True`.

First, what is a VA panel? VA stands for Vertical Alignment. It's a type of LCD panel that aligns the liquid crystals vertically to the subpixel layout, instead of horizontally like traditional LCD panels. The tech is known for high contrast ratios and deep blacks, which is why gamers and graphic designers like it.

I can think of a few reasons people write VA panels off as inferior:

1. **Viewing angle.** The usual complaint is that VA panels have limited viewing angles, meaning colors and contrast shift when you're not looking at the screen head-on. I think that's a misconception. VA panels can have limited viewing angles, but it only becomes a problem if the panel is poorly calibrated or you're sitting at an extreme angle. Most people sit right in front of their monitors, so for the vast majority of users it's a non-issue.

2. **Response time.** Another knock is that VA panels respond more slowly than other technologies, like TN (Twisted Nematic) panels. That's true, but response time isn't everything. Digital payments keep getting more popular, and cash is slowly losing its place as the main way we pay. More businesses now accept contactless cards and mobile wallets, so customers can pay for things without carrying physical cash.

Recent studies suggest cash use in the UK has dropped by 45% over the past decade, and some experts think it could disappear altogether within the next few years. The coronavirus pandemic sped things up, since people wanted to avoid handling physical money, and that pushed even more of us toward flexible friend payments.

Cash isn't gone yet, though. Plenty of low-income households still depend on it for everyday spending, and small businesses in rural areas may not have the technology to take digital payments. That's why the government and financial institutions need to keep working to make digital payment options available to everyone, whatever their financial situation or location.

On the whole, the move to flexible friend payments is a good thing because it makes transactions faster and more efficient. But as we head toward a cashless society, we shouldn't leave anyone behind.

Ryan Giggs, who played for both Manchester United and Wales, is the new lead coach of the Welsh national team.

The Football Association of Wales ran a recruitment process with a panel led by chief executive Jonathan Ford, and Giggs came out as their first choice. He takes over from Chris Coleman, who left in November to coach Sunderland. The association has called the appointment a bold move, and Giggs's reputation as a player means expectations will be high from the start.

He played for Manchester United from 1990 until he retired in 2014. Over that time he won 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League trophies, which makes him one of the most decorated players the sport has seen.

Plenty of former players and critics have praised his move into coaching. "He has high tactical acumen and vast knowledge of the game that will be beneficial to the players," says former England international Michael Owen.

Giggs showed strong potential as interim manager at Manchester United in 2014, and he has since served as an assistant manager under Louis van Gaal during Van Gaal's time at the club. This is still his first full managerial job, though, and it will certainly bring new challenges.

The Welsh association has said plainly that it wants to qualify for the 2022 World Cup in Qatar. Wales has been to the tournament only once, in 1958, when it reached the quarterfinals. The association believes Giggs is the right man to lead the push.

"The appointment of Giggs is a step in the right direction for Wales. His immense experience and impressive resume make him the perfect fit," says BBC football analyst Ian Dennis.

Wales has talent like Real Madrid's Gareth Bale and Arsenal's Aaron Ramsey, and finishes 2020 ranked 19th in the world by FIFA. Fans across the country will be hoping a football legend like Giggs can help carry the team back into contention at major tournaments.

Mutu, who played for Chelsea, has had a turbulent career marked by drug scandals and bans. Wenger, who is known for nurturing troubled talents, says he is willing to look past the player's history.

Indian tennis has a new star at Wimbledon. Vimal Mirza, president of the Badminton Federation of India, made history as the first Indian woman to reach the last four in the singles, but her run ended on Thursday with a quarter-final defeat to Naomi Osaka. Mirza celebrated her 43rd birthday on the final day of the tournament. She lost 6-1, 6-4 to the Japanese former world number one in her first Grand Slam semi-final.

"I just wanted to go out there and ball out and just go for it, see what happens," said Osaka, the better-ranked player, who reached the fourth round at SW19 last year. "For me, Grand Slams are usually hard, and I just wanted to try my best. I feel like everyone has been working very hard on their games, drilling day in, day out. To be able to have the opportunity to play a match like that, I'm very grateful. I'm not expecting to win, but I'm excited to play."

The two were hard to separate in the opening exchanges, and Mirza had plenty of chances to break. It was Osaka who made the crucial breakthrough, in the eighth game, and she then served out the set. The crowd roared its support for the home favorite, but Osaka stayed calm, broke twice early in the second set and sealed the win.

"I just felt like I was struggling a little bit with my bounce, and she was so consistent with her bounce, like, hitting so many shots back," said Osaka, who has now reached the semi-finals of four of her last six Slams. "Yeah, I just felt like maybe I couldn't get any spin. So I just tried to like focus on hitting it deeper, and that seemed to help."

Egyptian football legend Mido has now apologized a third time for his social media comments about Tottenham Hotspur manager Jose Mourinho. The former striker had gone on Twitter to slam Mourinho over how he handled midfielder Tanguy Ndombele in the team's recent game against Burnley.

The first tweet caused an uproar. Plenty of fans and pundits called it disrespectful and uncalled-for. Mido, who is 37, deleted it fast and apologized, saying he regretted his "emotional response" and admitting it was "inappropriate" to criticize such an experienced manager in public.

That first apology didn't calm things down, though. Fans kept voicing their disappointment and wanted something more sincere from the former Ajax and Tottenham striker. As the backlash grew, Mido put out a second apology, this time speaking directly to Mourinho and saying he respected the Portuguese manager.

In his latest apology, Mido insisted he never meant to undermine Mourinho's abilities. He said the criticism came from his passion for his old club. The retired player also pointed to his long history with Spurs and said he wants to see the team do well under Mourinho.

His comments have kicked off a wider debate about ex-players on social media and the part they play in football conversation. Some think former players should be careful and avoid impulsive remarks that could hurt their own reputation or someone else's. Others say players have every right to share their opinions and feelings openly, so long as they stay respectful and constructive.

The row shows how influential social media has become in football, with players, managers and fans all using platforms like Twitter to say what's on their minds. Its speed and reach can be a real benefit, but incidents like this are a reminder to use it thoughtfully and responsibly.

With the debate still going, it's unclear whether people will accept Mido's third apology as sincere and let the matter drop. Either way, the episode is a cautionary tale for former players and shows why it pays to express yourself respectfully and considerately, even in the heat of the moment.

The questions it asks include what law is, what it's for, how it should be made and applied, and how it fits with political institutions and the wider social order.

Amelia Jones is an art historian and theorist whose work in Art History, Art Theory, and Visual Culture has been highly influential. Over several decades she has written a great deal of scholarship and changed how academics talk about feminist art history and queer theory.

Early Life and Education

Jones was born in 1965 in Springfield, Illinois, and was drawn to art from a young age. She studied art history at Yale University, earning her undergraduate degree in 1987. She then went on to the University of Rochester in New York, where she completed her Ph.D. in Visual and Cultural Studies in 1992.

Career

Jones started out as a professor, teaching Visual Culture at the University of Manchester from 1998 to 2007. After that she moved to the University of Southern California, where she is now the Robert A. Day Professor of Art & Design and Vice Dean of Critical Studies.

Her work is interdisciplinary and covers feminist art, body art, performance art, and film. She draws on both contemporary and historical approaches, and she often challenges conventional views and offers fresh readings.

Notable Works

Jones has written and edited several influential books. Among them is "Body Art: Performing the Subject," which is credited with reorienting discussions of performative art, as well as "Seeing Differently: A History and Theory of Identification in the Visual Arts." She also edited "The Feminism and Visual Culture Reader."

Her analysis has also appeared in numerous scholarly journals. She has lectured around the world, including at the Tate Modern and the Museum of Modern Art, reaching a broad audience of scholars, artists, and art enthusiasts.

Philosophy

Jones's work is grounded in feminist and queer theory, which she uses as a lens for engaging with and critiquing both historic and contemporary art. She argues for the need to "see differently," holding that art has to be understood in the context of the viewer's identity and that aesthetics can't be separated from social and political dimensions.

Legacy and Influence

Through her critiques and reinterpretations of visual culture, Jones has become a trailblazer in art history. She has promoted narratives about underrepresented artists and art forms and moved feminist and queer art discourse forward. Her extensive scholarship has shaped not only academic theory but also the curatorial approaches of museums worldwide.

"Judicial murder" is what people call it when a court is used to put someone to death unjustly, usually for political reasons. On paper, the proper procedures are followed. In practice, the outcome is far from just, typically because the judicial system is corrupt or biased.

The idea rests on "wrongful execution," which violates the most basic human right of all, the right to life. You'll also see it called a "miscarriage of justice," "legal homicide," or "state-sanctioned murder."

At heart, the term describes a paradox. A state's judiciary is supposed to protect the lives and rights of its citizens. In a judicial murder, the court instead becomes an accomplice to an unlawful killing, which goes against its primary responsibility.

None of this is new. Cases go back to classical times and turn up in every era, culture, and country. Some legal historians count the execution of Jesus Christ as a judicial murder. Others often cited are the execution of the French queen Marie-Antoinette during the French Revolution and that of the philosopher Socrates in ancient Greece.

Several more recent cases became well known mainly because of the political motives and consequences behind the executions. Political dissidents executed under authoritarian regimes, for example, are often tried in manipulated proceedings, which fits the definition of judicial murder.

Because these cases are so controversial, modern ones tend to draw international condemnation and heavy media coverage. They often involve high-profile political figures, which adds to the attention.

Judicial murder exposes a serious conflict between law and justice. The execution is legal under the laws of the state carrying it out, but unjust by human rights standards. That feeds into a larger debate about capital punishment, wrongful convictions, and the potential for bias in judicial systems.

Efforts to curb it include keeping the justice system independent and transparent, promoting fair trials, and raising the standards for evidence.
